caption: The Orion Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A vast hollow of churning gas and dust fills the frame, sculpted into what look like plateaus, ridges and valleys, and sprinkled with more than 3,000 stars of many sizes. This is the Orion Nebula, the closest star-forming region to Earth, seen here in the sharpest view Hubble had ever made of it. Some of the stars in this picture had never before been spotted in visible light.

The bright centre holds the Trapezium, the nebula's four most massive stars, named for the four-sided pattern they make. Their ultraviolet light is hollowing out the cloud and stunting the growth of hundreds of smaller neighbours. Close by sit young stars still wrapped in disks of material, the raw ingredients of planetary systems, though they are too small to make out here.
Near the bottom, faint red points are brown dwarfs, objects too small to sustain nuclear fusion in their cores like the Sun. Hubble caught them here in visible light for the first time.
explore: At upper left glows M43, often called a miniature Orion Nebula because a single massive young star shapes it, rather than four. Dark pillars beside it point toward the Trapezium and are holding out against its erosive ultraviolet light. To the right, arcs and bubbles mark where winds of charged particles from the Trapezium stars slam into surrounding material.
The picture combines 520 Hubble images in five colours with ground-based photos, and the mosaic spans roughly the apparent size of the full Moon.

understand.summary: This mosaic comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters that span visible light and the near-infrared, including one that isolates the red glow of hydrogen. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The eye cannot see the near-infrared part of this data, and Hubble's long exposures record faint stars and brown dwarfs far too dim to see directly.

alt: A glowing cloud of dust and gas scattered with thousands of stars, bright at the centre, with a smaller glow at upper left, dark pillars, and faint red stars near the bottom.

caption: The star-forming region IC 348, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Thick clouds of gas and dust swirl across this scene, dotted with bright stars that each wear six long spikes, a pattern made by the optics of the telescope's mirrors. The densest knot of stars sits near the middle. This is IC 348, a star-forming region about 1000 light-years away, and the picture is one of the largest Webb has released to the public so far.

Hidden among the stars are brown dwarfs, objects smaller than the smallest true stars. Using the sensitivity of its Near-Infrared Camera, Webb hunted down the tiniest brown dwarfs in the region, some only about twice the mass of Jupiter.
No lighter brown dwarfs are known. That they exist at all is a puzzle, because current models of how stars form struggle to explain how such small objects can form in the same way that stars do.
explore: In the upper right, a handful of protostars are shooting out long, glowing jets. Where those jets have ploughed into the surrounding gas and dust they create bright patches known as Herbig-Haro objects, and this image offers an unusual view of them.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam. The two shortest-wavelength filters are shown in blue, the middle filter in green and the longest in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the human eye, so these colours are a translation of wavelengths we cannot see.

alt: Swirling clouds of gas and dust scattered with bright six-pointed stars, densest at the centre, with long glowing jets in the upper right.

caption: The Butterfly Nebula, NGC 6302, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two broad, glowing wings spread from a dark band that pinches the middle, their outer edges tinged with red and their inner parts laced with white. It looks like a delicate butterfly, but this is NGC 6302, a planetary nebula roughly 3800 light-years away in Scorpius, and it is anything but calm.

The wings are gas heated to nearly 20 000 degrees Celsius, racing outward at more than 950 000 kilometres per hour. At the centre is a dying star once about five times the Sun's mass. It has shed its outer layers over about 2200 years and now floods them with ultraviolet light, making them glow. Its surface temperature is estimated at over 220 000 degrees Celsius, yet the star itself is hidden inside a doughnut of dust, the dark band.
That dusty ring squeezes the outflow into an hourglass shape. Filters tuned to individual elements let astronomers read the gas's temperature, density and makeup.
explore: The red edges come mostly from nitrogen, tracing the coolest gas in view, while white areas glow with sulphur where fast gas crashes into slower material, making shock waves. Finger-like features pointing back at the star may be denser blobs resisting the wind.

The whole butterfly stretches more than two light-years, about half the distance from the Sun to Proxima Centauri. Before this stage, the star swelled into a red giant about 1000 times the Sun's diameter.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 took this in ultraviolet and visible light, using filters that isolate light from oxygen, helium, hydrogen, nitrogen and sulphur. The caption says the reddish edges trace nitrogen and the white regions trace sulphur.
understand.eye: Part of this data is ultraviolet light, which the eye cannot see, and each filter picks out a single chemical element's glow rather than the blended colour an eye would register.

alt: A butterfly-shaped nebula with two glowing wings, reddish outer edges and white patches, pinched at the centre by a dark band.

caption: The Helix Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: A blue-green glow fills the centre of this nebula, while farther out, beyond a ring of small knots, red light takes over. This is the Helix Nebula, also known as NGC 7293, photographed with the Wide Field Imager camera on the 2.2-metre Max-Planck Society/ESO telescope at La Silla in Chile.

The Helix is a planetary nebula: the outer layers of a dying star, cast off into space and lit up by the hot remnant left behind. Here that remnant is a central star of about 120 000 degrees Celsius. Its intense ultraviolet radiation, together with hot gas, makes oxygen atoms shine blue-green near the middle, while hydrogen and nitrogen give the outer parts their red colour.
Look closely at the central region and you can pick out not only the knots but also distant galaxies, visible straight through the thin, glowing gas.
explore: The picture was assembled from exposures through blue, green and red filters, lasting 12, 9 and 7 minutes respectively.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light colour composite from the Wide Field Imager, built from blue, green and red filter images. The caption ties the blue-green glow to oxygen and the red to hydrogen and nitrogen.
understand.eye: Exposures lasting several minutes gather far more light than the eye can, revealing faint gas and distant galaxies that would be invisible through an eyepiece.

alt: A nebula with a blue-green centre, a ring of small knots, and red outer regions.

caption: The Horsehead Nebula, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This colour picture shows the Horsehead Nebula together with the area immediately around it. The Horsehead is a dark nebula, a dense cloud of dust that blocks the light of glowing gas behind it, so it appears as a silhouette.

The view comes from the FORS2 multi-mode instrument on Kueyen, one of the 8.2-metre unit telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal. The picture was assembled from three frames taken on 1 February 2000 and later retrieved from the VLT Science Archive Facility, a reminder that archived data can keep producing new pictures.

Each frame captured a different slice of visible light. The blue-band exposure lasted 600 seconds, the green band 300 seconds and the red band 120 seconds, and the three were combined into a single colour composite covering the whole recorded field.
explore: The seeing during the observations was about 0.75 arcseconds, and each original pixel covers 0.2 arcseconds. The field shown spans roughly 6.5 by 6.7 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light composite from FORS2 on the Very Large Telescope. The B-band exposure is shown as blue, the V-band as green and the R-band as red.
understand.eye: Exposures of minutes on an 8.2-metre mirror collect far more light than the eye, so faint glowing gas and dust show up that would be invisible by eye.

alt: A colour image of the Horsehead Nebula and its immediate surroundings.

caption: The Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Rust-coloured columns rise through a multi-coloured glow of gas, threaded with wispy tendrils of dark dust. These are the Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula, returning in a fresh visible-light portrait from the Hubble Space Telescope, which revisited one of its most famous and popular images.

The pillars are clouds of gas and dust, the kind of material from which new stars form. They are under constant attack. Intense radiation from young stars scorches their surfaces, and strong winds from massive stars nearby wear them away.

That is what makes a second look so valuable. The new images bring better contrast and a clearer view than before, letting astronomers track how the pillars' shape shifts over the years. Comparing views taken years apart turns a single snapshot into something closer to a time-lapse of a nebula being slowly eroded.

understand.summary: This view comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in visible light, using filters that isolate the glow of oxygen, hydrogen and sulphur. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Each filter isolates one narrow band of light from a single element, so the colours are a scientific mapping, not the mix an eye would see, and the long exposures record gas far too faint to see directly.

alt: Rust-coloured pillars of gas and dust rising through a multi-coloured glow, with wispy tendrils of dark dust.

caption: Thor's Helmet Nebula, NGC 2359, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A helmet-shaped cloud of glowing gas gives this nebula its name. Thor's Helmet, also known as NGC 2359, lies around 15 000 light-years from Earth in the constellation Canis Major (the Great Dog), and it spans more than 30 light-years.

The helmet is really a bubble. A bright, massive star near its centre drives a wind, and as that wind rushes outward it sweeps up the surrounding molecular cloud, a cold reservoir of gas and dust, and inflates this cavity. The glowing structure traces where the star's wind is pushing into its surroundings.

This picture has a story of its own. It was taken with the Very Large Telescope to mark ESO's 50th anniversary, on 5 October 2012, with help from Brigitte Bailleul, the winner of ESO's Tweet Your Way to the VLT contest. Viewers could follow the observations online as they happened, in a live broadcast from Chile's Paranal Observatory.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: A large telescope's exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so the faint glowing bubble would not look like this by eye.

alt: A glowing, helmet-shaped bubble of gas surrounding a bright star near its centre.

caption: The Flame Nebula and surroundings, imaged by ESO's VISTA survey telescope
story: A star-forming cloud glows in this wide infrared view, with the reflection nebula NGC 2023 just below centre, the faint outline of the Horsehead Nebula towards the lower right, and a bright bluish star to the right. The main subject is the Flame Nebula, NGC 2024, in the constellation of Orion.

This was the first image released publicly from VISTA, described by ESO as the world's largest survey telescope. In visible light, thick dust completely hides the Flame's core. Infrared light slips through that dust, so here the cluster of very young stars at the nebula's heart comes into view.

That is the great strength of infrared astronomy for star formation: newborn stars usually sit deep inside the dusty clouds that formed them, where visible light cannot escape. That bright bluish star on the right belongs to the trio of bright stars forming Orion's Belt.
explore: The picture was made from exposures through the J, H and Ks near-infrared filters, with a total exposure time of 14 minutes. It covers about half of VISTA's full field, roughly 40 by 50 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from VISTA's VIRCAM camera, using J, H and Ks filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and by eye or in visible-light photos the Flame's core stays hidden behind dust.

alt: A glowing nebula with a cluster of young stars at its core, a smaller glow below centre, a faint horsehead outline at lower right, and a bright bluish star at right.

caption: The Omega Nebula, Messier 17, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: This is Messier 17, also called the Omega Nebula or the Swan Nebula, a sprawling region of gas, dust and hot young stars at the heart of our galaxy, in the constellation Sagittarius (the Archer). It was the first image released from the VLT Survey Telescope, or VST.

Star-forming regions like this are where clouds of gas collapse into new stars. The hot young stars that result pour out energy that makes the surrounding gas glow and shapes the clouds they were born from.

The VST was built to survey large patches of sky, and this picture shows why that matters. Its field of view is wide enough to take in the whole nebula, including its fainter outer parts, while staying sharp from edge to edge. The raw data were turned into this picture with Astro-WISE, software created by E.A. Valentijn with colleagues in Groningen and other institutions.

understand.summary: This image comes from the OmegaCAM camera on the VLT Survey Telescope, using filters in visible light and the near-infrared. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and long exposures pick up faint outer gas beyond what the eye could detect.

alt: A wide view of a large star-forming nebula of gas, dust and young stars.

caption: The Bubble Nebula, NGC 7635, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait shows the Bubble Nebula, also known as NGC 7635, an emission nebula about 8 000 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia. The telescope made this new image to celebrate its 26th year in space.

An emission nebula is a cloud of gas that shines with its own light. Energetic radiation from hot stars strips electrons from the gas atoms, and as those atoms settle back down they give off light at particular colours, which is why such clouds glow.

Hubble recorded this glow through filters that each let through the light of a single element: one for oxygen, one for hydrogen and one for nitrogen. Separating the light this way helps astronomers map where each kind of gas sits and how conditions vary across the cloud. The official caption offers few details beyond this, so the picture is best enjoyed as a celebration of the observatory's long working life.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters that isolate the glow of oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The narrow filters pick out individual elements' light, so the colours are a scientific mapping rather than what an eye would see, and the gas is far too faint to view this way directly.

alt: The Bubble Nebula, a glowing cloud of gas imaged by Hubble.

caption: Part of the Lagoon Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This colourful Hubble portrait zooms into a small corner of the Lagoon Nebula, a turbulent star-forming region about 4000 light-years away. The patch shown here is only about four light-years across. The telescope made this image to celebrate its 28th anniversary in space.

To put that in context, the whole nebula is about 55 light-years wide and 20 light-years tall, so this view captures just a sliver of it. Star-forming regions like the Lagoon are clouds of gas and dust in which new stars are taking shape, and the energy from those young stars stirs up and lights the surrounding gas, which is why such regions look so restless.

The Lagoon also has a long history on Earth. Italian astronomer Giovanni Battista Hodierna catalogued it in 1654, as part of an effort to record fuzzy objects in the night sky so that nobody would confuse them with comets.
explore: Since Hodierna's time, the Lagoon Nebula has been photographed and studied by many telescopes and astronomers around the world. Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 gathered the observations for this picture over about a week in February 2018.

understand.summary: This visible-light image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters that isolate the glow of oxygen, hydrogen and nitrogen, along with a broader visible filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The narrow filters pick out the light of individual elements, so the colours are a scientific mapping rather than what an eye would see, and the gas is far too faint to view like this directly.

alt: A colourful, turbulent region of glowing gas and dust within the Lagoon Nebula.

caption: The Carina Nebula, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: This detailed picture from the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory shows the Carina Nebula, a star-forming region in the southern constellation of Carina.

Star-forming regions like this one are vast clouds of gas and dust where new stars are born. The young, hot stars then light up and sculpt the clouds around them, creating the mix of glowing gas and dark dust typical of such nebulae. The telescope captured the scene through several broad colour filters and one tuned to the red glow of hydrogen, the most common element in these clouds.

The image also has a story behind it. Chile's then President, Sebastián Piñera, helped to take it when he came to Paranal on 5 June 2012. It was then released on 6 December 2012, when the new telescope was inaugurated in Naples. The official caption offers few details about the nebula itself, so the picture is best enjoyed as a showcase of what the new survey telescope could do.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the OmegaCAM camera on the VLT Survey Telescope, using broad colour filters plus a filter for hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures on a survey telescope gather much more light than the eye, so the faint gas appears far richer here than it would by eye.

alt: A detailed wide view of the Carina Nebula's gas and dust clouds.

caption: The Lion Nebula, NGC 2392, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A round nebula shaped like a lion's head floats against black space. At its centre a small pinkish-white star forms the lion's button nose, surrounded by purple-pink bubbles and rings that make up the face, while a thick purple-blue ring spreads around it like a mane. This is the planetary nebula NGC 2392, nicknamed the Lion Nebula.

The central star is a white dwarf, the exposed core of a dying star. It is so hot that its radiation is cooking the nebula from the inside, inflating a bubble of ionised hydrogen gas. Tendrils in that bubble are expanding and destroying dust as they go.

Some dust survives. The mane is the inside of a dust shell lit by the core, and compact clumps in it, shown in red and orange, are shielding material behind them. Yellow marks further clumps of molecular hydrogen.
explore: The nebula is a snapshot in time. Shaping the gas and dust like this has taken several thousand years, and the scene keeps changing as the star pushes material away. Astronomers estimate NGC 2392 will disperse in about 10,000 years, a short span in astronomical terms.
Distant galaxies, some with visible spiral arms, dot the background.

understand.summary: This near- and mid-infrared composite combines Webb's NIRCam and MIRI. The shortest filter is shown in blue, hydrogen light in cyan, molecular hydrogen in yellow, carbon-rich PAH molecules in orange and silicate dust at 10 microns in red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colours are assigned to wavelengths we cannot see.

alt: A round nebula shaped like a lion's head, with a pinkish-white star at the centre, purple-pink bubbles forming a face, and a thick purple-blue ring like a mane, against black space with distant galaxies.

caption: The reflection nebula Messier 78, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This colour portrait shows Messier 78, a reflection nebula in the constellation Orion. The camera behind it is the Wide Field Imager, mounted on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla in Chile.

A reflection nebula is a cloud of dust and gas that we see mainly because it scatters the light of nearby stars, rather than glowing on its own the way energised gas does. The effect is a little like fog lit up by a car's headlights: the cloud itself is dark, but starlight bouncing off its dust makes it visible.

Like most astronomical colour pictures, this one did not come from a single colour snapshot. It was built from many black-and-white exposures, each taken through a different filter: blue, yellow-green and red, plus one that isolates light from glowing hydrogen gas. Combining them recreates colour while also highlighting regions where hydrogen shines. The official caption gives little further detail about the nebula itself.
explore: The total exposure time for each filter was 9 minutes in blue, 9 minutes in yellow-green, 17.5 minutes in red and 15.5 minutes for the hydrogen filter.

understand.summary: This visible-light colour composite was made with the Wide Field Imager, using blue, yellow-green and red filters plus a hydrogen filter. The packet does not publish exactly which colour was assigned to each filter in the final picture.
understand.eye: Exposures lasting many minutes collect far more light than the eye, so this faint reflected glow looks much brighter here than it would through a telescope eyepiece.

alt: The reflection nebula Messier 78, a cloud of dust lit by nearby stars.

caption: Part of the Cat's Paw Nebula, NGC 6334, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Four roughly circular patches glow blue near the centre of this view, ringed by brown-orange filaments of dust that reach toward the edges. Small fiery red clumps are scattered through the dust, and many yellow-white stars dot the scene. This is a close-up of the Cat's Paw Nebula, NGC 6334, a massive star-forming region about 4,000 light-years away in Scorpius.

Webb looked at part of one of the nebula's rounded toe beans and found smaller toe-bean-like structures inside it, built from gas, dust and young stars. The image marked the telescope's third year of science.

The scene is chaotic and still unfolding. Massive young stars are eating into nearby gas and dust, and their light makes the blue glow. Because such stars are short-lived and very bright, they will eventually shut down star formation in this area.
explore: The Cat's Paw had already been studied by Hubble and the now-retired Spitzer space telescope. Astronomers return to it to understand the steps a turbulent molecular cloud goes through on its way to forming stars.
Near the top right corner sits a bright red-orange oval, and a few darker zones appear almost empty of stars.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam, with one filter at the edge of visible light. The shortest wavelengths are shown in blue and cyan, then green, yellow and orange, with molecular hydrogen at the longest wavelength shown in red.
understand.eye: Most of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and the eight-pointed spikes on bright stars come from Webb's optics, not the stars themselves.

alt: Four glowing blue circular patches surrounded by brown-orange dust filaments, with small red clumps and many yellow-white stars, some with eight-pointed spikes.

caption: The Tarantula Nebula and its surroundings, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: The spidery Tarantula Nebula sits in the upper centre of this wide view. A little to the lower right, a web of filaments surrounds the site of the famous supernova SN 1987A, and many other reddish nebulae are scattered across the frame. On the left lies a cluster of young stars called NGC 2100.

The whole scene covers one square degree of sky, a wide area for a detailed telescope image. It shows the Tarantula not in isolation but as part of a busy neighbourhood of star formation, with glowing clouds, young clusters and the remains of an exploded star all in one frame.

The picture was built from observations by Joao Alves, Benoit Vandame and Yuri Beletsky using the Wide Field Imager on the 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla. It is a two-by-two mosaic, combining broad blue and visual filters with narrow filters that capture the glow of hydrogen and of oxygen.
explore: ESO's Advanced Data Products group did the first processing of the data, using the ESO/MVM pipeline.

understand.summary: This visible-light mosaic from the Wide Field Imager combines B and V broad-band filters with narrow-band H-alpha and oxygen filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures and narrow filters bring out faint glowing gas that would be far too dim, and not so colourful, to the eye.

alt: A wide field with the spidery Tarantula Nebula at upper centre, a web of filaments at lower right, several reddish nebulae, and a star cluster on the left.

caption: The Carina Nebula, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This broad view shows the Carina Nebula, a southern-sky region where massive stars are forming, seen in infrared light by the HAWK-I camera on ESO's Very Large Telescope. Across a landscape of gas, dust and young stars, many features that were previously hidden have come into view.

The reason is the kind of light used. In visible light, thick clouds of dust block much of what lies inside and behind them. Infrared light passes through dust far more easily, so an infrared camera can reveal stars and structures that ordinary photographs miss.

That makes infrared especially useful in star-forming regions, where young stars are often still wrapped in the dusty clouds that gave birth to them. Seeing through the dust lets astronomers count those stars and study how they are forming. The official caption offers few further details, but the image shows how a change of wavelength can turn a familiar nebula into a new landscape.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from HAWK-I on the Very Large Telescope, taken through J, H and Ks filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and in visible light much of what appears here would be hidden behind dust.

alt: An infrared view of the Carina Nebula showing gas, dust and many young stars.

caption: The star-forming region around R Coronae Australis, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This picture shows the nearby star-forming region surrounding the star R Coronae Australis. It was taken with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.

Star-forming regions are clouds of gas and dust in which new stars are taking shape. Being nearby makes this one easier to study in detail, because astronomers can pick out finer structure than they could in more distant clouds.

The field is generous. It covers 33.7 by 31.9 arcminutes, roughly the diameter of the full Moon, so the scene would take up about as much sky as the Moon does. To build it, astronomers combined twelve CCD frames of 67 megapixels each, taken through blue, visual and red filters, with four exposures of five minutes each. The official caption says little about the region's structure, so the image stands mainly as a wide, detailed portrait of a nearby stellar nursery.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filter exposures. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Several minutes of exposure per frame collect far more light than the eye, so faint dusty clouds appear that would be invisible by eye.

alt: A wide view of the star-forming region around the star R Coronae Australis.

caption: The Cat's Paw Nebula, NGC 6334, imaged by ESO's VISTA survey telescope
story: This infrared view from VISTA shows the Cat's Paw Nebula, NGC 6334, a vast star-forming region about 5500 light-years away in the constellation Scorpius. The whole gas cloud spans about 50 light-years.

Among the nurseries of young massive stars in our galaxy, NGC 6334 is one of the busiest. Some of its stars are nearly ten times the mass of the Sun, and most were born within the last few million years, which is very recent by cosmic standards.

Looking in infrared helps because such young stars are often buried in dust that blocks visible light. Infrared light slips through much more easily, revealing stars and structure that would otherwise stay hidden. VISTA is built to survey wide areas, and this field is about one degree across, which lets the whole sprawling nebula fit in a single frame.
explore: The picture was made from exposures through the Y, J and Ks filters, five minutes each, shown as blue, green and red respectively.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from VISTA's VIRCAM camera combines Y, J and Ks filters, shown as blue, green and red respectively.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so these colours stand in for wavelengths we cannot see, and dust that looks opaque in visible light becomes more transparent.

alt: An infrared view of the Cat's Paw Nebula, a large star-forming cloud with many young stars.

caption: The stellar nursery Sharpless 29, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: This glittering view shows Sharpless 29, a stellar nursery captured by the OmegaCAM imager on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope. Many different astronomical phenomena can be spotted in this giant image.

Chief among them are clouds of cosmic dust and gas interacting with the light of hot young stars inside the nebula in three different ways. Some clouds reflect that light, scattering it toward us much as fog scatters a lamp's glow. Others absorb it, appearing as dark patches where dust blocks what lies behind. And some re-emit it: the gas soaks up energetic starlight and then shines with its own glow.

Seeing all three effects in one picture makes Sharpless 29 a useful example of how young stars shape their surroundings. The images were taken through filters spanning visible and near-infrared light, including one designed to catch the glow of hydrogen and nitrogen. The official caption offers few further details about the region itself.

understand.summary: This image comes from OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope, using visible and near-infrared filters, including one for hydrogen and nitrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and long exposures record faint clouds that would be invisible by eye.

alt: A glittering stellar nursery of dust and gas clouds lit by hot young stars.

caption: The nebulae NGC 2014 and NGC 2020, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble portrait features the giant nebula NGC 2014 alongside its neighbour, NGC 2020. The pair belong to a sprawling region of star birth in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy orbiting the Milky Way. The image counts among the most photogenic of the many turbulent stellar nurseries Hubble has observed over its 30-year lifetime.

A stellar nursery is a cloud of gas and dust in which new stars are forming. Once the most massive of those stars switch on, their intense radiation and winds heat, light and push around the surrounding gas, which is why such regions look so restless and full of structure.

Hubble recorded this scene through a mix of filters: broad ones spanning visible light and the near-infrared, and narrow ones tuned to the glow of oxygen and of hydrogen and nitrogen. The narrow filters pick out where particular kinds of gas are shining. The official caption offers little more detail, so this picture is best enjoyed as a celebration of Hubble's three decades in space.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, combining broad visible and near-infrared filters with narrow filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the narrow filters highlight specific elements rather than the colours an eye would see.

scaleExtra: The Large Magellanic Cloud lies approximately 163 000 light-years away, according to the caption.
alt: The nebulae NGC 2014 and NGC 2020, a turbulent star-forming region imaged by Hubble.

caption: The Red Spider Nebula, NGC 6537, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Two large loops of blue molecular gas stretch diagonally away from a blotchy pinkish centre, where strong red light illuminates the dust, all set against thousands of whitish stars. This is NGC 6537, the Red Spider Nebula, a planetary nebula seen in new detail by Webb.

Planetary nebulae form when Sun-like stars die. After swelling into red giants, they shed their outer layers, exposing white-hot cores whose ultraviolet light makes the cast-off gas glow. This stage lasts only a few tens of thousands of years.

Webb revealed the full extent of the spider's legs for the first time: closed bubbles, each about 3 light-years long, traced by glowing hydrogen molecules. The central star, faint and blue in Hubble's view, shows up red here because Webb detected hot dust around it, probably orbiting in a disc. A hidden companion star may explain the narrow waist and wide lobes.
explore: A purple S shape through the centre traces glowing iron atoms, marking where a fast jet from near the central star has crashed into material the star shed earlier, sculpting the rippling structure.
The observations belong to a joint Chandra and Webb programme studying how outflows and jets shape bipolar planetary nebulae.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam. Light from iron is shown in blue, molecular hydrogen in cyan, a 3.56-micron filter in orange and hydrogen's Brackett-alpha line in red.
understand.eye: This infrared light is invisible to the eye, which is why the central star, faint and blue in visible light, can appear red here.

alt: A planetary nebula with a blotchy pinkish centre glowing red, two large blue loops extending diagonally to the corners, and many whitish background stars.

caption: The Horsehead Nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Along the bottom of this view curves a wall of dense, smoky dust and gas, a close-up of the top of the Horsehead Nebula. Above it, distant stars and galaxies fill a background that fades from dark red to black, while one bright star throws six long spikes across the frame. These are the sharpest infrared images of the Horsehead to date.

Also called Barnard 33, the nebula lies roughly 1300 light-years away in Orion. It formed from a collapsing cloud and glows because a nearby hot star lights it. The surrounding gas has already dispersed, but the pillar's thick clumps resist erosion; astronomers estimate it has about five million years left.

The Horsehead is a photon-dominated region, where ultraviolet light from massive stars heats a mostly neutral layer of gas and dust and drives its chemistry. Being close and almost edge-on, it is ideal for studying how radiation interacts with interstellar matter.
explore: Such regions form where gas is dense enough to stay neutral but not so dense that far-ultraviolet light cannot get in. Their light helps astronomers trace how interstellar matter evolves, in our galaxy and across cosmic history.
Webb's view sits in the western part of the Orion B molecular cloud.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam. Shorter filters, including one for methane, are shown in blue; water ice and molecular hydrogen in cyan; PAH molecules in green; carbon dioxide in orange; and molecular hydrogen and hydrogen's Brackett-alpha line in red.
understand.eye: This light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the image translates chemistry and warmth into colours we can see.

alt: A curved wall of smoky gas and dust along the bottom, with distant stars and galaxies above and one bright star with six long spikes, against a background fading from dark red to black.

caption: The Omega Nebula, Messier 17, imaged by ESO's New Technology Telescope
story: This three-colour picture shows the Omega Nebula, also known as Messier 17 or NGC 6618. It was assembled from images recorded by EMMI, an instrument on ESO's 3.58-metre New Technology Telescope, which stands at La Silla in Chile.

The Omega Nebula is a star-forming region: a cloud of gas and dust in which new stars are being born, and in which the energy from young stars makes the surrounding gas glow. This particular view is a close-up. On the sky it spans roughly a third of the full Moon's width, which at the nebula's distance works out to roughly 15 light-years across.

One detail matters for anyone comparing it with other photographs: the picture is oriented with north pointing down and east to the right, so it may look flipped relative to other views of the same object.

understand.summary: This visible-light composite from EMMI on the New Technology Telescope uses B, V and R filters, shown as blue, green and red.
understand.eye: The telescope's exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the nebula's faint gas shows much more clearly here than it would by eye.

alt: A three-colour image of the Omega Nebula's glowing gas and dust.

caption: The Orion Nebula and its surroundings, imaged by ESO's VISTA survey telescope
story: This wide infrared view shows the Orion Nebula, Messier 42, which is about 1350 light-years from Earth. ESO's VISTA, an infrared survey telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile, took the picture.
VISTA's huge field of view meant the whole nebula and its surroundings could fit in a single picture. That lets astronomers see the nebula and its wider setting together.

Its infrared vision matters just as much. The Orion Nebula is a place where stars are forming, and many of its youngest stars are buried inside dusty regions that visible light cannot pass through. Infrared light slips through that dust, so VISTA can peer into the normally hidden clouds and show what the lively young stars inside are up to. Views like this help astronomers see how star formation unfolds across an entire region at once, rather than one patch at a time.
explore: The picture was built from images in the near-infrared, through Z, J and Ks filters, with ten minutes of exposure per filter. It covers an area of sky of about one degree by 1.5 degrees.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from VISTA's VIRCAM camera combines Z, J and Ks filter images. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and much of what VISTA shows inside the dust would be hidden in visible light.

alt: A wide infrared view of the Orion Nebula and surrounding clouds.

caption: The Treasure Chest in the Carina Nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: At the centre of this view, the thickest clouds take the shape of a chest whose lid has been thrown open, glowing from within and breaking into long pillars of thick gas at its base. Dark orange globules and pale hazes fill the background. This feature, aptly named the Treasure Chest, lies in the Carina Nebula, about 7500 light-years away.

It is a cometary globule: a lone cloud with a thick, dark head trailing a long, sweeping tail. Its treasure is a compact cluster of about 70 young stars, whose light makes the glow. The most massive is a rare O-type star roughly 19 times the Sun's mass.

At an age of likely around 1.3 million years, the cluster is still embedded in dust, and many of its stars appear to have discs around them. Radiation and winds from massive stars nearby, including Eta Carinae, largely shaped the cloud.
explore: Eta Carinae, the most luminous object in the Carina Nebula, sits just 39 light-years to the northwest on the sky. One of its stars alone shines about 5 million times brighter than the Sun. The likeliest story is that the cluster formed first in a larger cloud, and feedback from nearby stars then swept away the thinner gas.
The Carina Nebula spans roughly 260 light-years and also holds the Cosmic Cliffs.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam. A 1.62-micron filter is shown in blue, iron light in cyan, a 4.44-micron filter in orange and molecular hydrogen in red.
understand.eye: This light is infrared, so the eye could not see it, and Webb's sensitivity reveals the glow from stars buried inside the dust.

alt: Dense clouds shaped like an open chest glowing from within, with long pillars at its base, dark orange globules and pale hazes behind, and bright foreground stars.

caption: The star cluster Pismis 24, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A blue and black sky filled with stars of white, beige, yellow and light orange covers the top two thirds of this scene. Below rises a craggy, mountain-like landscape in orange, yellow and brown, with spire-like peaks and misty valleys, topped by a wispy white cloud. It looks like a starlit mountaintop, but it is really a landscape of dust being eaten away by the fierce winds and radiation of nearby massive young stars.

Those stars belong to Pismis 24, a young cluster at the heart of the nearby Lobster Nebula, some 5,500 light-years away in Scorpius. The region holds a vibrant stellar nursery and is one of the closest sites where massive stars are being born.
That closeness makes Pismis 24 valuable. It gives rare insight into large, massive stars and is one of the best places to explore how hot young stars behave and evolve.
explore: In the top right corner, a swath of orange and brown material cuts diagonally across the sky.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam, with one filter at the edge of visible light. The shortest wavelengths are shown in blue, then cyan and green, with PAH molecules in orange and molecular hydrogen in red.
understand.eye: Most of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the mountain's colours are a translation of wavelengths we cannot see.

alt: A star-filled blue and black sky above a craggy orange, yellow and brown mountain-like landscape of dust, topped by a wispy white cloud.

caption: The Orion Nebula, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This picture of the Orion Nebula star-formation region was built from multiple exposures with the HAWK-I infrared camera on ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile. It is the deepest view ever made of this region.

Depth here means sensitivity to faint objects. By combining many exposures, astronomers could detect things too dim to show up in shallower images. And the result held a surprise: more very faint planetary-mass objects than expected. These are bodies with masses in the range of planets.

Infrared light helps in two ways. It passes through much of the dust that hides young objects in visible light, and small, cool bodies give off most of their light at infrared wavelengths anyway. The official caption gives few other details.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from HAWK-I on the Very Large Telescope, using J, H and Ks filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the faint planetary-mass objects would be far too dim to see even with a large telescope's eyepiece.

alt: A deep infrared view of the Orion Nebula star-forming region.

caption: Barnard 59 in the Pipe Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This highly detailed picture features Barnard 59, a section of a vast dark cloud of interstellar dust known as the Pipe Nebula. Barnard 59 forms the mouthpiece of the pipe.

The Pipe is a dark nebula. Instead of glowing, it shows up as a shadow: its dust is thick enough to block the light of the stars behind it, so it appears as a dark shape against the stars behind it. Clouds like this are cold and dense, the kind of places where new stars can eventually form.

The camera was the Wide Field Imager, mounted on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. It is so large that ESO strongly recommends the zoomable version to appreciate it fully, since much of the detail only emerges at full size. The filters used spanned visible light and the near-infrared. The caption offers few other details.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and I filters, spanning visible light and the near-infrared. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the long exposures reveal far more background stars than an eye could see.

alt: Barnard 59, part of the Pipe Nebula, a vast dark cloud of interstellar dust.

caption: Part of the Orion Molecular Cloud OMC-2, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Layers of blue, green and yellowish gas and dust fill this scene, broken by thick clumps of cold dust so dark they block all light. Stars from small and orange to large and white or blue sit among the clouds, while streams of glowing whitish gas mark where jets from young stars strike their surroundings. This is a small northern part of OMC-2, 1280 light-years away, just behind and north of the Orion Nebula.
All the stages of star birth appear in this scene, which spans just 2.5 light-years: stellar embryos, protoplanetary discs and newly formed stars.

The earliest stage is the protostar, a growing star fed with gas through a spinning disc. Infalling gas heats up and makes it glow, and the energy escapes as twin jets from its poles. Here those jets drive shockwaves that heat the gas into sharp, glowing red ridges.
explore: Visible light from OMC-2 is blocked by the dust around the Orion Nebula and by its own clouds, so only in infrared do the protostars start to shine through. By following the outflows, you can hunt for protostars still too buried to see directly.
The data come from a programme studying star formation in OMC-2 and its neighbour OMC-3.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam maps shorter filters to blue and cyan and longer ones to green and red. The caption says blue and cyan hazes are scattered starlight, yellow to green is mostly PAH emission, orange, brown and some red mark warmer dust, and red ridges are outflow-heated gas.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared, and in visible light the region's dust would hide the protostars completely.

alt: Layers of blue, green and yellowish gas with dark clumps of dust, stars of varying size and colour, and streams of glowing whitish gas from young stars' jets.

caption: The Orion Nebula and its star cluster, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: This detailed view shows the Orion Nebula together with its cluster of young stars, captured by OmegaCAM, the wide-field optical camera on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope.

The Orion Nebula is a famous object and the birthplace of many massive stars. At a distance of about 1350 light-years, it counts among the nearest stellar nurseries. A stellar nursery is a cloud of gas and dust in which new stars are taking shape, and the energy from the young stars lights up the surrounding gas.

The cluster and the nebula belong together: the stars formed from the cloud, and their radiation now shapes and illuminates what remains of it. OmegaCAM's wide field lets both fit in one frame. The picture was taken through filters spanning visible light and the near-infrared, including one tuned to the red glow of hydrogen. The official caption offers little more detail, so this view is best taken as a portrait of a nearby stellar nursery.

understand.summary: This image comes from OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope, using visible and near-infrared filters plus one for hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and long exposures bring out faint gas that would be invisible by eye.

scaleExtra: The nebula lies about 1350 light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: The Orion Nebula's glowing gas and its cluster of young stars.

caption: The planetary nebula NGC 6072, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A mostly red cloud with a lopsided, splattered shape glows around a bright central star, like paint thrown on the ground. At its heart, a light blue glow falls over darker blue pockets traced with orange, and the shells turn deeper red farther out. This is the planetary nebula NGC 6072, seen by Webb in near-infrared light.

A planetary nebula is the gas a dying star sheds late in its life. Here the scene is complicated: several outflows expand at different angles from the central star, pushing gas toward the star's equatorial plane, where it forms a disc.

That messy, irregular look is itself a clue. Astronomers suspect that at least one other star is interacting with the material the dying star has thrown off, and that this companion is responsible for the nebula's unusual shape.
explore: The red areas in this image represent cool molecular gas, such as molecular hydrogen. Behind the nebula, the black background is speckled with tiny stars and distant galaxies.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam, with one filter at the edge of visible light. The shortest filter is shown in blue, then cyan, green, yellow and orange, with molecular hydrogen at the longest wavelength in red.
understand.eye: Most of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colours translate wavelengths we cannot see.

alt: A mostly red, asymmetric cloud shaped like splattered paint around a bright central star, with a light blue centre and darker pockets, against a black background with tiny stars.

caption: The Lupus 3 dark cloud and nearby young stars, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This picture shows two stages of the same story side by side: a dark cloud where new stars are forming, and a group of brilliant stars that have already broken free of the dusty nursery that made them. The cloud is Lupus 3, which lies roughly 600 light-years away, in Scorpius (the Scorpion).

Dark clouds like this are dense pockets of dust and gas. The dust blocks starlight, which is why the cloud looks dark, while inside it gravity pulls material together until new stars ignite. Once those stars grow bright enough, they can clear away their surroundings and become visible, like the brilliant stars nearby.

There is a personal connection too. Astronomers think it is likely the Sun formed in a similar star-forming region more than four billion years ago. ESO's MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla in Chile took the picture, which ESO calls the finest view yet of this little-known cloud.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters with a filter for sulphur light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, revealing faint dust and background stars that would not be visible by eye.

alt: A dark cloud of dust beside a cluster of brilliant young stars.

caption: The light echo around V838 Monocerotis, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the star V838 Monocerotis, or V838 Mon, surrounded by dusty clouds whose lighting has changed dramatically. The effect is known as a light echo.

In early 2002 the star suddenly brightened for several weeks. The flash of light then travelled outward through the dust around the star. Because light takes time to cross space, it reaches different parts of the cloud at different times, and each part lights up as the flash passes through and reflects some of it toward us. The result is like a sonar sweep that gradually lights up the surroundings layer by layer.

That is why the view keeps changing. Ever since the outburst, the echo has been revealing dust patterns that had never been seen before, as the light reaches ever more distant parts of the cloud. Hubble's repeated images let astronomers watch that process unfold. The official caption offers few other details, so this picture is best read as one frame in an evolving sequence.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the reflected light from the dust is far too faint to see without a long telescope exposure.

alt: The star V838 Monocerotis surrounded by illuminated clouds of dust.

caption: Part of the Helix Nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: In this close-up, thousands of orange and gold pillars shaped like comets rise from the bottom edge, as if thin liquid had been blown up across a pane of glass. They are densest and darkest red at the bottom, where they form part of an arcing shell, and grow thinner and more golden higher up. This is a small section of the Helix Nebula, the expanding shell of gas and dust around a dying star.
Webb's image highlights these comet-like knots, along with fierce stellar winds and layers of gas that the dying star has shed. All of that material is interacting with the space around it.
The picture also captures an abrupt shift from the hottest gas to the coolest as the shell spreads outward from the central white dwarf, the small, hot core the star left behind.
explore: Bright blue stars dot the scene, a few of them showing diffraction spikes, with a few larger ones on the right side. The black of space shows through between the thinner pillars at the top.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam shows the two shortest filters in blue, the next two, including molecular hydrogen, in green, and the two longest, including molecular hydrogen, in red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colours are a mapping of wavelengths we cannot see.

alt: Thousands of orange and gold comet-like pillars streaming upward from an arcing shell at the bottom, with bright blue stars scattered across a black background.

caption: The Serpens Nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Layers of wispy gas and dust in orange, red and blue fill this young stellar nursery. In the upper left, amid mostly orange dust, several small red plumes all point the same way, and at the centre a bright star sits within an hourglass-shaped shadow. This is the Serpens Nebula, 1 300 light-years from Earth, in a view from Webb's Near-InfraRed Camera.
Those red streaks are the key finding. They are shockwaves where jets from young stars slam into surrounding gas, and they form a group of aligned outflows in one small corner of the nebula.

The Serpens Nebula holds an especially crowded cluster of stars still forming, around 100 000 years old, and some will eventually grow to the mass of the Sun. The hourglass at the centre is the flapping Bat Shadow, named after Hubble data from 2020 revealed it shifting.
explore: To the right of the Bat Shadow is an eye-shaped crevice that looks as if a star is bursting through. Astronomers caution it may simply be gas of different densities layered on top of each other, as in the Pillars of Creation. Farther right, a very dark patch may be dust so dense that no near-infrared light gets through.
The black rectangles at two corners mark missing data.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam shows a 1.4-micron filter in blue, a 2.1-micron filter in cyan, a 3.6-micron filter in orange and a 4.8-micron filter in red.
understand.eye: This light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and some of the densest dust here blocks even infrared light.

alt: Wispy orange, red and blue gas and dust, with small red plumes at upper left, a bright central star with an hourglass shadow, an eye-shaped crevice to its right, and black rectangles of missing data at two corners.

caption: The Red Spider Nebula, NGC 6537, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble picture shows the Red Spider Nebula, NGC 6537, a two-lobed planetary nebula in the constellation of Sagittarius. According to the caption, it lies some 3000 light-years away. The nebula is sculpted by huge waves.

A planetary nebula forms from the outer layers of a dying star, cast off into space and lit up by the hot core left behind. This warm example holds one of the hottest stars known, and that star's powerful winds drive waves 100 billion kilometres high.

The waves are supersonic shocks. As the lobes expand rapidly, they compress and heat the gas in front of them, much as a fast-moving boat piles up water at its bow. Atoms caught in these shocks give off the radiation that makes the nebula visible in this image, so what we see is essentially a map of where the gas is being struck. The official caption offers no details about the filters or colours used.

understand.summary: This is a Hubble image, but the packet gives no instrument or filter information and does not publish the colour mapping.
understand.eye: Long telescope exposures gather far more light than the eye, so this faint glowing gas would not look like this by eye.

alt: A two-lobed planetary nebula with wave-like structures in its glowing gas.

caption: The Ring Nebula, Messier 57, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble captures the striking form and colours of the Ring Nebula, also known as Messier 57, in this image. The Ring is a planetary nebula: the cast-off outer layers of a dying star, lit up by the hot core left behind.

From Earth, the Ring looks like a simple ellipse with a ragged edge. Its real shape is more interesting. By combining existing ground-based data with new Hubble observations, astronomers discovered that the nebula has the form of a warped doughnut. Slotted into the doughnut's central gap is a rugby-ball-shaped region of thinner material, stretching toward and away from us.

This is a good example of how perspective can fool us. We see a three-dimensional object squashed onto the flat sky, so a doughnut viewed nearly end-on can pass for a ring. Only by piecing together different observations can astronomers work out the true form. Hubble used a wide range of filters here, each isolating light from a particular element, which helps reveal how gas is arranged throughout the nebula.

understand.summary: This visible-light image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using many narrow filters that isolate light from hydrogen, helium, oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The narrow filters separate the light of individual elements in a way the eye cannot, and long exposures record gas far too faint to see directly.

alt: The Ring Nebula, Messier 57, a planetary nebula imaged by Hubble.

caption: The Crab Nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Fluffy magenta dust forms a cage-like structure around this supernova remnant, clearest toward the lower left and upper right. Yellow-white mottled filaments loop around its centre, and ghostly blue wisps, like smoke, gather toward the middle. This is the Crab Nebula, the debris of an exploded star, dissected by Webb.

Using NIRCam and MIRI, astronomers mapped the warm dust throughout the remnant for the first time. Dust filaments thread the interior and sometimes coincide with doubly ionised sulphur, shown in green; where the two overlap, the filaments look yellow-white.

The blue glow is synchrotron emission, produced by charged particles spiralling in magnetic fields. Thin blue ribbons follow the field lines created by the Crab's pulsar, a rapidly rotating neutron star at its heart. The dust cage helps contain some of this emission, but not all. These data help astronomers test leading theories of the remnant's origins.

understand.summary: This combines Webb's NIRCam and MIRI in near- and mid-infrared light. Synchrotron emission is shown in blue, doubly ionised sulphur in green and warm dust in magenta, with overlapping dust and sulphur appearing yellow-white.
understand.eye: This is infrared light invisible to the eye, so the colours map physical ingredients rather than anything a viewer could see.

alt: A supernova remnant with a cage of fluffy magenta dust, yellow-white looping filaments, and smoky blue wisps near the centre.

caption: The Trifid Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Dark bands of dust cut across the glowing heart of this nebula, dividing it into three parts. That is where the Trifid Nebula gets its name. This massive star factory was photographed with the Wide Field Imager camera on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in northern Chile.

The Trifid is unusual because it combines three types of nebula in one. Textbooks usually sort them this way: emission nebulae, where gas glows because young stars energise it; reflection nebulae, where dust scatters nearby starlight; and dark nebulae, where dense dust blocks light from behind. Having all three together makes the Trifid a rare case.

Together they show the violence of newly born stars and hint that more stars will form, since the dusty regions hold material for future stars. The image covers a field of approximately 13 by 17 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters with a hydrogen filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the nebula's colours and faint gas are much more vivid here than through an eyepiece.

alt: A glowing nebula divided into three parts by dark bands of dust.

caption: The supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A roughly circular cloud of gas and dust fills the frame. Its inner shell is built from bright pink and orange filaments, dotted with knots that resemble fragments of broken glass, and wrapped in curtains of wispy material like smoke from a campfire. This is Cassiopeia A, or Cas A, the remains of a star that exploded, in a high-definition view from Webb's NIRCam.

Those pink and orange knots contain sulphur, oxygen, argon and neon that came from the star itself. Only NIRCam's fine resolution can pick them out, and they hint at how the star shattered like glass in the explosion.

The smoky outskirts show where material blasted out by the explosion is slamming into gas the star shed before it died. Researchers conclude that this white glow is synchrotron radiation, made by very fast charged particles spiralling around magnetic field lines.
explore: Several light echoes also appear, most clearly in the bottom right corner. There, light from the long-ago explosion has reached distant dust and warmed it, and the dust glows as it cools. Clumps of dust outside the nebula are coloured yellow, and stars show as blue and white points.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam. The caption explains that the pink and orange knots are gas from the star and the white glow is synchrotron radiation, but the full filter-to-colour mapping is not published in the packet.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the colours here translate wavelengths we cannot see.

alt: A roughly circular supernova remnant with a bright pink and orange inner shell of knotted filaments, wrapped in smoky wisps, with yellow dust clumps outside and blue and white stars.

caption: The young star system FS Tau, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Transparent blue and purple clouds of gas and dust stretch from just left of centre toward the right edge, with yellow and white protostars scattered through them, some wearing Webb's eight-pronged spikes. Orange wisps reach from a central protostar toward opposite corners, and distant galaxies dot the black background. This is the young star system FS Tau.

Protostars are baby stars that condense out of dense pockets of gas and dust. Hot, clumpy and low in mass, they will eventually burn hydrogen in their cores like the Sun. Those in FS Tau are only about 1 to 3 million years old, compared with the Sun's 4.6 billion years.

FS Tau A, a pair of protostars about half the Sun's mass, makes the largest spike pattern just left of centre. FS Tau B, the orange protostar right of centre, is thought to drive the red and orange outflows.
explore: The red outflows are molecular hydrogen and the orange ones are soot-like molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Blue ridges mark light scattered by dust.
Background galaxies' colours reveal the dust in front of them: redder ones lie behind more dust, yellower ones behind thinner layers, and whiter ones are mostly unobstructed.

understand.summary: This is an infrared image from Webb's NIRCam, with one filter at the edge of visible light shown in blue, then cyan, green, orange for two filters including PAH molecules, and red for molecular hydrogen.
understand.eye: Most of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and the eight-pointed spikes on bright objects come from Webb's optics.

alt: Transparent blue and purple clouds with yellow and white protostars, orange wisps extending toward the top left and bottom right, and distant galaxies on a black background.

caption: The Pencil Nebula, NGC 2736, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This picture shows the oddly shaped Pencil Nebula, catalogued as NGC 2736. The camera responsible is the Wide Field Imager, mounted on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla site in Chile.

The Pencil is not an isolated cloud. It is a small piece of a much larger remnant left behind after a supernova, the explosion of a star, which took place about 11 000 years ago. When a massive star explodes, it flings its material outward at high speed, and as that debris ploughs into the thin gas between the stars it compresses and heats it, making it glow.

The image was recorded through several broad colour filters and one that isolates the red glow of hydrogen, which highlights the heated gas. The official caption offers few further details about the nebula.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters with a hydrogen filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so this faint glowing filament would not look like this by eye.

alt: The oddly shaped Pencil Nebula, a small part of a supernova remnant.

caption: The Medusa Nebula, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This colourful cloud is the Medusa Nebula, also known as Abell 21 and Sharpless 2-274, in the most detailed image ever taken of it, captured by ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile.

The Medusa is the work of a star in its final stage. As the star at the nebula's heart entered retirement, it threw its outer layers off into space, and that material now forms the glowing cloud. Objects like this are called planetary nebulae; the name is historical and has nothing to do with planets. The hot exposed core left behind lights up the surrounding gas.

There is a personal angle to this view. The image is a glimpse of the Sun's distant future, because the Sun will also eventually become an object of this kind, casting off its outer layers and leaving a small, hot remnant behind. The telescope recorded the nebula through broad colour filters and narrow ones for oxygen and hydrogen light.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the FORS2 instrument on the Very Large Telescope, using B, V and R filters plus filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures on an 8-metre-class telescope collect far more light than the eye, so this faint nebula looks much richer than it would by eye.

alt: The Medusa Nebula, a colourful cloud of gas shed by a dying star.

caption: The variable star RS Puppis, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows RS Puppis, an ethereal star wrapped in its dusty surroundings and set against a dark sky dotted with background galaxies.

RS Puppis is a Cepheid variable, a type of star that regularly swells and shrinks, changing in brightness as it does. Compared with other variable stars, Cepheids take a long time to complete a cycle. RS Puppis, for instance, changes in brightness by almost a factor of five, completing each cycle in roughly 40 days.

What makes this star unusual is its setting. It is enveloped in thick, dark clouds of dust, and those clouds allow a phenomenon called a light echo to show up with exceptional clarity. As the star's brightness rises and falls, each pulse of light travels outward and lights up different layers of dust at different times, so the pattern around the star keeps shifting. Hubble's sharp view captures that effect in detail.

understand.summary: This visible-light image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue and visible filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The dusty glow around the star is far too faint to see by eye; only long telescope exposures reveal it.

alt: A bright star surrounded by dusty clouds, set against a dark sky with background galaxies.

caption: The cometary globule CG4, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Like the gaping mouth of a huge creature, the cometary globule CG4 glows in this image from ESO's Very Large Telescope.

A cometary globule is a cloud of gas and dust with a dense head and a long, faint tail, so called because the shape can resemble a comet. In this picture, CG4 looks large and bright. That impression comes from the telescope, not the object: CG4 is actually a faint nebula and is not easy to observe. A large telescope gathering light over long exposures can bring out detail that would otherwise stay hidden.

The most intriguing part of CG4's story is what we do not know. The exact nature of this globule remains a mystery, and the official caption offers no firm explanation for how it formed or what shapes it. The picture was recorded through several broad colour filters and one that isolates the red glow of hydrogen, but beyond that the object keeps its secrets.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the FORS1 instrument on the Very Large Telescope, using B, V and R filters plus a hydrogen filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: CG4 is faint, so it would look nothing like this by eye; the long exposures on a very large telescope make it appear bright.

alt: The cometary globule CG4, a glowing cloud that resembles a gaping mouth.

caption: The Herbig-Haro object HH 797, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A narrow, brightly coloured nebula stretches across the lower half of this view, while above it a glowing point radiates multi-coloured light in every direction. This is HH 797, a Herbig-Haro object lying near the young star cluster IC 348, on the eastern side of the Perseus dark cloud complex.

Herbig-Haro objects form when winds or jets from newborn stars smash into nearby gas and dust at high speeds, creating shockwaves that glow. Infrared light escapes the dust around such young stars, so Webb's NIRCam can trace the hot, shocked molecules in the outflows.

Ground-based studies had found a velocity pattern across HH 797 that astronomers once put down to the outflow rotating. Webb's sharper view shows that the single outflow is really two almost parallel ones, each with its own shocks. So the source is not one star but two, each driving its own jet.
explore: The bright infrared objects in the upper part of the image are thought to host two more protostars, and another outflow comes from a protostar top right of centre, with its lit cavity walls. HH 797 lies directly north of HH 211, which featured in a Webb release in September 2023.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam shows iron and a 1.5-micron filter in purple, molecular hydrogen and methane at about 2 microns in blue, molecular hydrogen at 3.23 microns in cyan, PAH molecules in green, carbon monoxide in orange and molecular hydrogen at 4.7 microns in red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and the young stars' outflows would be hidden by dust in visible light.

alt: A narrow, brightly coloured horizontal nebula across the lower half, a glowing point radiating multi-coloured light above, and a bright star with long spikes at the right edge.

caption: The stellar nursery RCW 120, imaged by the APEX telescope with optical survey data
story: Blue clouds surround a reddish glow in this colour composite of RCW 120. The reddish glow is ionised gas, and the blue clouds are cold material seen at submillimetre wavelengths.

The picture tells a story of stars triggering the birth of more stars. A growing bubble of ionised gas, roughly ten light-years wide, is pushing into the material around it and causing it to collapse into dense clumps. New stars then form inside those clumps.

The image combines several data sets. The submillimetre observations, at a wavelength of 870 microns, came from the LABOCA camera on the 12-metre Atacama Pathfinder Experiment (APEX) telescope. Light at that wavelength is emitted by cold dust, which is why it traces the dense clumps so well. The reddish ionised gas comes from the SuperCosmos H-alpha survey, while the Second Generation Digitized Sky Survey adds visible and near-infrared images.

understand.summary: This composite combines submillimetre data from APEX's LABOCA camera, shown as blue clouds, with H-alpha survey data showing the ionised gas in red, and Digitized Sky Survey images with the I-band in blue and the R-band in red.
understand.eye: Submillimetre light is completely invisible to the eye, so the blue clouds show material we could never see directly.

alt: A reddish glowing bubble of ionised gas surrounded by blue clouds.

caption: Part of the Veil Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble zooms in here on a small piece of the Veil Nebula, the famous remnant of a supernova. The part pictured lies in the nebula's outer shell, in a region called NGC 6960, or more informally the Witch's Broom Nebula.

A supernova remnant is what is left after a massive star explodes. The blast sends material racing outward, and as it ploughs into the thin gas between the stars, it compresses and heats that gas until it glows. Over time this forms a vast, expanding shell, often laced with delicate filaments, and the Veil is a well-known example.

This view isolates just one piece of that shell, showing it in much finer detail than wide-field views can. Its observations used filters that isolate the glow of oxygen, sulphur and hydrogen alongside broader visible and near-infrared filters, which helps separate the glow of different gases. The official caption offers little further detail, so this view is best enjoyed as a close look at the edge of an exploded star's debris.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, combining filters for oxygen, sulphur and hydrogen light with broad visible and near-infrared filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the filaments are far too faint to see in this detail without long exposures.

alt: Glowing filaments of gas in a section of the Veil Nebula.

caption: Part of the Monkey Head Nebula, NGC 2174, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This colourful region, filled with young stars embedded in bright wisps of gas and dust, belongs to NGC 2174, nicknamed the Monkey Head Nebula, which sits about 6400 light-years away in Orion (the Hunter). Hubble released the image to celebrate its 24th year in orbit.

Young stars and bright clouds belong together here. Stars form inside clouds of gas and dust, and once they switch on, their energy lights up and sculpts the material around them, giving regions like this their glowing, ragged look.

What sets this view apart is the kind of light used. Hubble imaged this part of the nebula in infrared with its Wide Field Camera 3. Infrared light passes through dust more easily than visible light, so it can show stars and structures that would otherwise be hidden. Hubble had already observed this part of the sky in 2011, making this image a return visit.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, taken through Y, J and H filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the colours here are a translation of wavelengths we cannot see.

alt: A colourful region of bright gas and dust wisps with young stars embedded inside.

caption: The planetary nebula Abell 33, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A blue bubble, almost perfectly round on the sky, lines up with a bright star. The pairing looks uncannily like a diamond engagement ring. This is the planetary nebula Abell 33, captured by astronomers using ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile.

The bubble formed when an ageing star blew off its outer layers. After a Sun-like star runs low on fuel, it sheds its outer gas into space, and the hot core left behind makes that gas glow. The name planetary nebula is a historical accident from early telescopes and has nothing to do with planets.

Two things make Abell 33 special. First, the diamond is a coincidence: the bright star is in the foreground and just happens to fall in line with the bubble from our point of view. Second, the nebula is unusually symmetric, appearing almost perfectly circular on the sky.
