understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the FORS2 instrument on the Very Large Telescope, using B, V and R filters plus filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures on a large telescope collect far more light than the eye, so this faint bubble appears much brighter and more colourful than it would by eye.

alt: A nearly circular blue bubble aligned with a bright foreground star, resembling a diamond ring.

caption: The planetary nebula ESO 378-1, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A glowing bubble floats in the darkness of space like the ghost of a star. It may look supernatural, but it is a familiar kind of object: a planetary nebula, the remains of a dying star. This one is catalogued as ESO 378-1, and the picture, captured by ESO's Very Large Telescope in northern Chile, is the best view of this little-known object yet obtained.

Planetary nebulae form near the end of a Sun-like star's life. The star puffs off its outer layers of gas, and the hot, exposed core left behind floods them with energetic light, making them glow. Despite the name, these objects have nothing to do with planets; the term dates back to their round, planet-like look in small telescopes.

The telescope recorded the scene through broad colour filters and narrow ones tuned to the glow of oxygen and hydrogen, which trace where these gases shine in the shell. The official caption offers few further details about this particular nebula.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the FORS2 instrument on the Very Large Telescope, using B, V and R filters plus filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: This faint bubble would be very hard to see by eye; the long exposures on a large telescope bring out its glow.

alt: A glowing, ghostly bubble of gas against the dark of space.

caption: The Sagittarius C region near the Milky Way's centre, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: In a field crowded with stars, a dark funnel-shaped region with fewer stars widens toward the top of the frame. Near its narrow end, a small red and white clump sends streamers up and to the left, while a bright cyan area curls around the lower funnel in a rough U. This is Sagittarius C, or Sgr C, in the dense centre of the Milky Way. An estimated 500,000 stars shine here.

The dark funnel is an infrared-dark cloud, so dense that it blocks light from stars behind it. The cyan is ionised hydrogen, which researchers were surprised to find extends about 25 light-years, laced with needle-like structures pointing in no set direction.

At the base of the cloud, a cluster of protostars is producing outflows that glow like a bonfire. These still-growing stars seem to be emerging from their protective cocoon and will soon take their place among the more developed stars nearby.
explore: Smaller dark clouds are scattered around, looking like holes punched in the starfield. The research team says it has barely started to explore these high-resolution data, and many features, including the rose-coloured clouds on the right side, have never been seen in such detail.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam shows a 1.62-micron filter in blue, hydrogen's Brackett-alpha line in cyan, a 3.6-micron filter in orange and molecular hydrogen in red.
understand.eye: This light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colours stand in for wavelengths we cannot see.

scaleExtra: The full view spans a portion of the Milky Way's centre about 50 light-years wide, according to the caption.
alt: A starry field with a dark funnel-shaped cloud, a small red and white clump sending out streamers, a bright cyan U-shaped glow, and orange and red clouds with a purple haze on the right.

caption: The star formation region Gum 15, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This richly detailed picture shows the glowing cloud Gum 15, a star formation region in the constellation of Vela (the Sails). ESO's MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, Chile, captured it.

Gum 15 is a little-known object, but a fine example of an HII region. That is the name astronomers give to a cloud of hydrogen gas that has been ionised, meaning the energetic light of hot young stars has stripped electrons from its atoms. When the electrons and atoms recombine, the gas glows, typically in a reddish colour from hydrogen.

The caption also notes a resemblance between Gum 15 and a more famous HII region, the Trifid Nebula, also known as Messier 20. Both are places where young stars are lighting up the clouds they formed in. The picture was taken through blue and red filters and one that isolates the glow of hydrogen, which highlights the ionised gas. The official caption offers few further details.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B and R filters with a hydrogen filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the glowing hydrogen appears much more vivid than it would by eye.

scaleExtra: Gum 15 lies some 3000 light-years from Earth, according to ESO.
alt: Gum 15, a glowing cloud of gas in a star-forming region.

caption: The central region of Gum 15, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A smoky black silhouette winds through a red-tinged frame in this close-up. It is part of Gum 15, a large, sparse cloud of partially ionised hydrogen, known as an HII region, and the view zooms in on one of its dust lanes at the nebula's centre.

The dark patches seem to hold few stars because dust hides the glowing gas behind them. The few stars that do show up there lie between us and Gum 15, creating the illusion of a window onto the more distant sky.

The cloud is shaped by strong winds from stars within and around it. It sits near several large groups of stars, including a star cluster whose brightest member, HD 74804, is thought to have ionised Gum 15's hydrogen, and it is this ionised hydrogen that gives the whole frame its red hue. In wider images the nebula looks like a reddish purple clump slashed by dark, winding dust lanes.
explore: This image came from the ESO Cosmic Gems programme, which uses telescope time unsuitable for science to make images for education and outreach, with the data archived for astronomers. It used the FORS instrument on the Very Large Telescope. ESO had already released a wider view of Gum 15 in July 2014, and this region sits in its top left quarter.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the FORS2 instrument on the Very Large Telescope, using B, V and R filters plus a hydrogen filter. The caption says the red hue comes from ionised hydrogen; the full filter-to-colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Long exposures on a large telescope gather much more light than the eye, so the faint red glow looks far stronger here than it would by eye.

alt: A smoky black lane of dust winding through a red-tinged field of glowing gas, with a few foreground stars.

caption: The star-forming region NGC 346, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Arcs of bluish material form a boat-like shape across the lower half of this image, while another plume of blue filaments rises from the centre toward the top left, like a sailboat's mast. Translucent pink curtains cover most of the scene, and stars are noticeably scarce. This is NGC 346, seen in mid-infrared light by Webb's MIRI instrument.

Mid-infrared light traces cool gas and dust rather than starlight, which is why so few stars appear. Here, blue shows silicates and sooty molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs. The softer red glow comes from warm dust, warmed by the region's brightest, most massive stars at its heart.

The bright patches and filaments are of special interest, because they mark places crowded with protostars. A couple dozen bright pink patches with short six-pointed spikes sit among the blue filaments, and many faint blue dots speckle the dark background.
explore: Five MIRI filters went into the picture, each assigned its own colour, running from 7.7 microns at the short end to 21 microns at the long end.

understand.summary: This is a mid-infrared image from Webb's MIRI. The 7.7-micron filter is shown in blue, 10 microns in cyan, 11.3 microns in green, 15 microns in yellow and 21 microns in red.
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is completely invisible to the eye, and it shows glowing dust rather than the stars an eye would pick out.

alt: Bluish arcs forming a boat-like shape with a blue plume like a mast, translucent pink curtains across the scene, bright pink patches with short spikes, and faint blue dots on a dark background.

caption: The R Coronae Australis region, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This colour photograph shows the region around R Coronae Australis, in the southern part of the Milky Way. It was obtained with the Wide Field Imager camera on the 2.2-metre MPG/ESO Telescope at La Silla in Chile, and the field covers about 33.7 by 31.9 arcminutes, close to the diameter of the full Moon.

The observations were made on the night of 30 August 2000. The picture was built from a series of CCD exposures through blue, visual and red filters, which were then shown as blue, green and red to recreate colour.

Producing it took careful work. The camera's detector is made of eight separate CCD chips with gaps between them, so the telescope took exposures at slightly different positions to fill in those gaps. All the frames were then aligned and their brightness levels adjusted to get the colour balance right, and a logarithmic brightness scale was used so that both faint and bright areas show up well.
explore: The image combines twelve large CCD frames of 8000 by 8000 pixels, with four five-minute exposures in each filter. The full field was scaled down to make it easier to share online. The images were prepared by Fernando Comeron of ESO.

understand.summary: This visible-light composite from the Wide Field Imager uses B, V and R filters, rendered as blue, green and red respectively.
understand.eye: Several exposures of minutes each gather far more light than the eye, and the logarithmic scaling reveals faint regions an eye would miss.

alt: A colour view of the R Coronae Australis region in the southern Milky Way.

caption: The Helix Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Kitt Peak 0.9-metre telescope
story: A red and blue ring of gas is threaded with a fine web of spoke-like filaments, and thousands of comet-like strands along its inner rim point back to a tiny central star. This is the Helix Nebula, one of the nearest planetary nebulae to Earth, in one of the largest and most detailed images of a celestial object ever made.

The portrait is really a look down a tunnel of glowing gas about a trillion miles long. Because the tube points almost straight at Earth, it resembles a bubble rather than a cylinder. The central star is a small, super-hot white dwarf.

The comet-like strands formed when a hot wind of gas from the star ploughed into colder shells of dust and gas it had thrown off earlier. They may lie in a disk around the star, like a collar. Blue marks glowing oxygen, and red marks hydrogen and nitrogen.
explore: Hubble's time for this came during the November 2002 Leonid meteor storm. Controllers turned the telescope away from the meteor stream, and the Helix happened to lie almost opposite, so Hubble spent nine orbits photographing it. Those images were blended with a wide view from the Mosaic Camera on Kitt Peak's 0.9-metre telescope.
Through binoculars, the Helix looks like a ghostly, greenish cloud in Aquarius.

understand.summary: This combines Hubble Advanced Camera for Surveys images with a wider Kitt Peak Mosaic Camera photo in visible light. The caption says blue represents glowing oxygen and red represents hydrogen and nitrogen.
understand.eye: Through binoculars the Helix appears only as a ghostly greenish cloud; the fine streaks need very large telescopes to resolve.

alt: A red and blue ring of glowing gas with fine spoke-like filaments and many comet-like strands along its inner rim, around a small central star.
flags: distance conflict: caption 650 ly vs metadata 2500 ly

caption: The Southern Ring Nebula, NGC 3132, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Jagged rings of gas and dust surround a bright central star, pierced by hundreds of straight, brightly lit lines that stream through gaps in the nebula like sunlight through breaks in a cloud. The centre is set off in teal, and transparent red regions reveal distant galaxies behind. This is NGC 3132, the Southern Ring Nebula, a planetary nebula seen by Webb in near-infrared light.

The bright central star is not the nebula's source. That role belongs to a second, dimmer star, which you can just make out at lower left on one of the bright star's spikes. Over thousands of years it has cast off at least eight shells of gas and dust.

The two stars are locked in a tight orbit. As they circle each other, the dimmer star sprays material in many directions, while the brighter one stirs up turbulence. Together they create these intricate rings.
explore: Deeper teal in the centre marks denser gas and dust that light cannot escape. The bright angled line at upper left is not starlight but a faraway galaxy seen edge-on, and the smallest, reddest galaxies are the most distant or the dustiest.
NIRCam was built by the University of Arizona and Lockheed Martin's Advanced Technology Center.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam shows a 0.9-micron filter in blue, hydrogen's Paschen-alpha line in cyan, molecular hydrogen at 2.12 microns in green, a 3.56-micron filter in yellow, and hydrogen's Brackett-alpha line with molecular hydrogen at 4.7 microns in red.
understand.eye: Most of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and the diffraction spikes on bright stars come from Webb's optics.

alt: Jagged rings of gas around a bright central star, crossed by straight bright lines, with a teal centre and red outer regions dotted with distant galaxies.

caption: Part of the star-forming region Messier 17, imaged by ESO's 3.6-metre telescope
story: Red stars, bluer stars, a diffuse glow and dark patches fill this colour-coded infrared view of the south-western part of Messier 17, a star-forming region in our galaxy.

Each colour tells you something. Red objects are young stars heavily hidden by dust. Bluer ones are either stars in the foreground or well-developed massive stars whose intense light ionises the hydrogen around them. The diffuse glow almost everywhere comes from hydrogen atoms forming again as protons and electrons recombine. The dark areas are where thick dust blocks the light of objects behind it, and that same dust makes many stars look redder.

Infrared shows what visible light cannot. In the upper left sits a cluster of young stars so deeply buried in the nebula that it cannot be seen in optical light, yet it shows up clearly here. The images were taken with the SOFI camera on ESO's 3.6-metre telescope.
explore: Exposures of five minutes each were made through J, H and Ks filters, with another 15 minutes on separate sky frames. The field covers about 5 by 5 arcminutes, roughly 3% of the full Moon, with north up. Objects in the far upper left corner look slightly stretched because of an optical effect at the edge of the field.

understand.summary: This near-infrared composite from SOFI uses J, H and Ks filters, rendered as blue, green and red respectively.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the buried star cluster in the upper left cannot be seen at all in visible light.

alt: An infrared field of red and blue stars with diffuse glowing gas and dark dusty patches, and a cluster of young stars in the upper left.

caption: The Orion Bar region of the Orion Nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Layers of colourful, cloudy material fill this scene. The upper left is brightly lit and full of thin wisps in pale pink and blue, while a thick, denser bar of orange material cuts diagonally across the lower right, fading darker toward the corner, where two very bright stars sit with long spikes. This is the Orion Bar, part of the Orion Nebula, seen by Webb's NIRCam.

The region is bathed in harsh ultraviolet light from the Trapezium Cluster. That radiation erodes gas and dust through photoevaporation, carving the cavities and filaments seen here, and it makes molecules glow so astronomers can study them.

Here, Webb data revealed the methyl cation, CH3+, for the first time, in the disc around a young star called d203-506. Its key role in interstellar carbon chemistry had been predicted since the 1970s, and it turned up where life-friendly planets might one day form.
explore: The two bright stars belong to the θ² Orionis system. The brightest, θ² Orionis A, is surrounded by bright red puffs of dust reflecting its light, and it is visible to the naked eye because it is itself three tightly bound stars.
In the top left, a tiny star sits inside a long dusty cocoon made from its own eroding disc, with a round shockwave moving through the gas around it.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam uses many filters, running from purple and blue for the shortest wavelengths through cyan, green, yellow and orange to red for the longest, including filters for molecular hydrogen, water ice and PAH molecules.
understand.eye: This light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colours map wavelengths and chemistry we cannot see.

alt: Colourful layers of cloudy material, with pale pink and blue wisps at upper left, a thick orange bar crossing the lower right, and two very bright stars with long spikes.

caption: The supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A roughly circular nebula glows inside a square frame turned about 45 degrees. Orange curtains of material wrap its outer edge, a ring of mottled bright pink filaments studded with knots lies inside, and a greenish loop reaches into the central cavity from the right. This is Cassiopeia A, or Cas A, a supernova remnant about 11,000 light-years away, seen in mid-infrared light by Webb's MIRI.
The orange and red curtains, strongest at the top and left, come from warm dust. They mark where debris from the exploded star is slamming into material the star shed earlier.

The pink filaments are material from the star itself, probably glowing from a mix of heavy elements and dust. The green loop is the puzzle: its shape and complexity are unexpected, and scientists are still working to understand it.
explore: The remnant spans approximately 10 light-years. Fainter wisps of stellar material also appear near the inside of the cavity, and translucent threads of blue, green and red run through the whole image.

understand.summary: This is a mid-infrared image from Webb's MIRI. Red is assigned to 25.5 microns, orange-red to 21, orange to 18, yellow to 12.8, green to 11.3, cyan to 10, light blue to 7.7 and blue to 5.6 microns.
understand.eye: Mid-infrared light is invisible to the eye, so these colours show the heat of dust and gas rather than anything we could see.

alt: A circular nebula in a rotated square frame, with glowing orange outer curtains, a ring of mottled bright pink filaments, a greenish loop into the central cavity, and translucent wisps of blue, green and red.

caption: The Wolf-Rayet star WR 124, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A large, bright star blazes at the centre with Webb's characteristic diffraction spikes, surrounded by a clumpy cloud that is thicker above and below than at the sides and turns yellow closer to the star. This is Wolf-Rayet 124, or WR 124, a luminous, hot, ageing massive star, in a combined near- and mid-infrared view.

The cloud is gas and dust thrown off by the star, stretching 10 light-years across. Its structure is a record of past episodes of mass loss. Instead of smooth shells, it formed through random, lopsided ejections.

Bright clumps look like tadpoles swimming toward the star, their tails blown back by the stellar wind. The two instruments worked together: NIRCam balanced the star's glare against the fainter gas and dust, while MIRI revealed the nebula's structure. Background stars and galaxies peek through the gaps.
explore: The star's spikes are not real features of WR 124. They arise from the way the telescope itself is built, and they are a signature of Webb's images.

understand.summary: This combines Webb's NIRCam and MIRI. Red is assigned to 4.44, 4.7, 12.8 and 18 microns, green to 2.1, 3.35 and 11.3 microns, and blue to 0.9, 1.5 and 7.7 microns.
understand.eye: Almost all of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and the spikes around the star are an artefact of the telescope, not something in space.

alt: A large bright star with diffraction spikes at the centre, surrounded by a clumpy cloud, yellow near the star, with more material above and below, and background stars.

caption: The Herbig-Haro object HH 211, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A thin, multi-coloured cloud tilts across the centre from bottom left to top right. At its middle is a dark brown cloud from which two outflows burst in opposite directions, shading from yellow and orange to light blue, with pale pink features at the outer ends. This is Herbig-Haro 211, a bipolar jet racing through space at supersonic speeds, about 1,000 light-years away in Perseus.

Few outflows from young stars are as young or as close to us. It comes from a Class 0 protostar, a baby version of the Sun when it was only a few tens of thousands of years into its life, with just 8% of the Sun's present mass.

Webb reveals the bow shocks and narrow jet at roughly 5 to 10 times the resolution of earlier images. The inner jet wiggles in mirror symmetry on either side, a hint that the protostar may be an unresolved binary.
explore: Newborn stars stay wrapped in the gas of the cloud that formed them, but infrared light from their outflows gets through. Molecules stirred up in the turbulence, including molecular hydrogen, carbon monoxide and silicon monoxide, give off infrared light that Webb uses to map the outflow.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam shows iron and a 1.62-micron filter in purple, methane and molecular hydrogen filters in blue, PAH molecules in cyan, carbon monoxide in green and orange, and molecular hydrogen at 4.7 microns in red.
understand.eye: This light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and the young star is hidden by gas that visible light cannot penetrate.

alt: A thin multi-coloured cloud tilted from bottom left to top right, with a dark brown centre and two outflows shading from yellow-orange to light blue, with pink features at the ends.

caption: The Tarantula Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and ESO's New Technology Telescope
story: Just above the centre of this mosaic sits R136, a huge cluster of very hot stars, while near the lower edge lies an older cluster, Hodge 301, wrapped in filaments and sheets of gas. This is the Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a smallish irregular galaxy 170,000 light-years away. Even without a telescope, the nebula shows up as a big, milky smudge.

The stars in R136 are among the most massive known, and the cluster is young: its oldest stars are only about 5 million years old, and its smallest are still forming. Hodge 301 is almost 10 times older. Some of its stars have already exploded as supernovae, and the shockwave compressed nearby gas into the filaments seen around it.

Astronomers believe the Large Magellanic Cloud is in a violent phase. Close encounters with the Milky Way, which it orbits, are thought to have triggered a burst of star formation, part of which we see here.
explore: The mosaic was created by 23-year-old amateur astronomer Danny LaCrue from 15 exposures by Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, laid over matching images from ESO's New Technology Telescope at La Silla. Each Hubble exposure lasted between 800 and 2800 seconds per filter.

understand.summary: This visible-light mosaic uses three narrow-band filters from Hubble's WFPC2: ionised oxygen shown as blue, hydrogen-alpha shown as green and ionised sulphur shown as red.
understand.eye: An eye would see hydrogen's glow as red, not green, and the narrow filters separate individual elements in a way the eye cannot.

alt: A colourful nebula with a dense cluster of bright stars just above centre and an older star cluster near the lower edge surrounded by filaments of gas.

caption: The Cat's Paw Nebula, NGC 6334, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This portrait shows the Cat's Paw Nebula, NGC 6334, a vast star-forming region about 5500 light-years away in Scorpius. The whole gas cloud spans about 50 light-years, and it appears strongly red.

That red colour has two causes. The red light comes mainly from hydrogen gas lit up by the fierce light of hot young stars. On top of that, the material between the nebula and Earth scatters and absorbs blue and green light more efficiently than red, much as dust and haze redden a sunset.

NGC 6334 ranks among our galaxy's busiest nurseries of massive stars and has been studied extensively. It hides freshly formed brilliant blue stars, each nearly ten times the Sun's mass and born within the last few million years. It is also home to many baby stars buried deep in dust, which makes them hard to study. Altogether, the Cat's Paw may hold several tens of thousands of stars.
explore: The picture was made with the Wide Field Imager on the 2.2-metre MPG/ESO telescope at La Silla in Chile, combining blue, green and red filters with a special filter that lets through the light of glowing hydrogen.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines blue, green and red filters with a hydrogen filter. The caption explains that the red comes mostly from glowing hydrogen; the full filter-to-colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the nebula's red glow is much more vivid here than through a telescope eyepiece.

alt: A large, strongly red nebula of glowing gas and dark dust scattered with stars.

caption: The star-forming region NGC 346, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Wispy gas surrounds a star cluster like a cobweb in this view of NGC 346, the brightest star-forming region in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy some 210,000 light-years from Earth. Found in Tucana (the Toucan), it measures approximately 200 light-years across.
The cobweb has a clear cause. Light, wind and heat from the cluster's massive stars have pushed and scattered the glowing gas in and around it, sculpting the delicate nebula that surrounds the stars.

Pictures like this help astronomers chronicle how stars are born and evolve, and show how that development changes the look of the surroundings over time. The image was obtained with the Wide Field Imager on the 2.2-metre MPG/ESO telescope at La Silla in Chile, and its field of view is about 30 arcminutes wide.

understand.summary: This enhanced-colour visible-light image combines B, V and R broadband filters with a narrowband hydrogen-alpha filter, which is shown in blue. The mapping for the other filters is not published.
understand.eye: Here the hydrogen glow, which the eye would see as red, is shown in blue, and long exposures reveal faint gas an eye would miss.

alt: A star cluster surrounded by wispy, cobweb-like glowing gas.

caption: The star-forming region NGC 2467, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Huge clouds of gas and dust, sprinkled with bright blue, hot young stars, look like a bubbling cauldron in this Hubble view of NGC 2467. Strangely shaped dust clouds, resembling spilled liquids, stand out as silhouettes against a colourful glowing background.

NGC 2467 is a star-forming region, much like the familiar Orion Nebula. This enormous cloud, made mostly of hydrogen, acts as an incubator for new stars. As those stars switch on, their energy makes the surrounding gas glow, while denser pockets of dust block the light and appear dark.

The colours carry chemical information. Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded the scene through three filters chosen to pass different shades of red and yellow light, each given off by different elements in the gas. Mapping them into colour shows where those elements are glowing. The combined exposure time was about 2000 seconds.
explore: The whole scene spans roughly 3.5 arcminutes of sky.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Its three filters, F550M, F660N and F658N, are shown in blue, green and red respectively, and each passes red or yellow light from particular elements.
understand.eye: The filters capture only red and yellow light, so the blue and green here are assigned colours rather than what an eye would see.

alt: Huge clouds of gas and dust with bright blue young stars and dark, oddly shaped dust clouds silhouetted against a colourful glowing background.

caption: The supernova remnant N103B, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Orange-red filaments form a shell near the top of this Hubble image, while glowing gas fills the lower half and a dense gathering of stars crowds the lower left. The shell is SNR 0509-68.7, also known as N103B, the remains of a Type Ia supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a galaxy next door to our own.

The orange-red filaments trace the shock fronts of the explosion. They let astronomers work out where the explosion originally happened. They also show that the remnant is no longer expanding as a sphere but has become elliptical. Astronomers assume that part of the ejected material ran into a denser cloud of interstellar gas, slowing it down, and the fact that the shell is open on one side supports this idea.
Because N103B is relatively close to Earth, astronomers study it to search for a possible stellar survivor of the explosion.
explore: The glowing gas below and the crowd of stars at lower left belong to the fringes of NGC 1850, a star cluster Hubble has imaged in the past.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using visible and near-infrared filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the faint filaments would not be visible without a long telescope exposure.

alt: An orange-red shell of filaments near the top, glowing gas in the lower half, and a dense concentration of stars at lower left.

caption: The stellar nursery around NGC 2467, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Pink regions of glowing gas, spread across the frame like a colourful ghost or a giant mandrill's face, surround several clusters of stars. This is the area around the star cluster NGC 2467, in the southern constellation of Puppis (the Stern).

No more than a few million years old, this is a busy stellar nursery in which stars are still being born from large clouds of dust and gas. The pink areas are vast regions of ionised gas, lit up by the energetic light of young stars.

Look for the landmarks. The open cluster Haffner 18 sits at the centre, and Haffner 19 lies at middle right inside a smaller pink region, the mandrill's lower eye. At the centre of the largest pink region, at the bottom of the image, shines HD 64315, a massive young star that plays a part in shaping the structure of the whole nebula. The image was taken through a wide range of filters, from ultraviolet through visible light, including ones for oxygen and hydrogen.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager combines ultraviolet, B, V and R filters with narrow filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is ultraviolet, invisible to the eye, and long exposures bring out faint gas that would be invisible by eye.

alt: Pink regions of glowing gas around several star clusters, resembling a ghost or a mandrill's face, with a bright star at the centre of the largest pink region at the bottom.

caption: The young star pair Herbig-Haro 46/47, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A thin orange cloud tilts across the centre from bottom left to top right. At its heart, huge red and pink eight-pointed diffraction spikes surround a yellow-white blob that hides two tightly orbiting stars, still forming. They are Herbig-Haro 46/47, seen in near-infrared light by Webb. A disc of gas and dust around them keeps adding to their mass.
The pair are only a few thousand years old, very young given that stars take millions of years to form. That helps researchers learn how stars gather mass, and perhaps model how the Sun formed.

The orange lobes come from earlier outbursts, and newer ejections show as blue threads along one angled spike. When forming stars swallow material too fast, they fire twin jets along the opposite axis, slowing their spin and shedding mass. Over millennia these outbursts control how much mass the stars keep.
explore: A delicate, semi-transparent blue nebula surrounds the pair, and Webb sees through its gauzy layers. Where jets ram into it at lower left, they spread wider and light up. Its edges form a soft orange outline, like a backward L.
In the background, blue objects with spikes are stars, white-and-pink spirals are far more distant galaxies, and the tiniest red dots are often the oldest, most distant galaxies.

understand.summary: This is a composite of several near-infrared exposures from Webb's NIRCam. The caption explains what the colours show, orange lobes from earlier ejections and blue threads from recent ones, but the filter-to-colour mapping is not published in the packet.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it lets Webb see through the gauzy nebula to stars and galaxies far behind it.

alt: A thin orange cloud tilted from bottom left to top right, with large red and pink eight-pointed diffraction spikes around a yellow-white central blob, against a background of stars and galaxies.

caption: Part of the Iris Nebula, NGC 7023, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thick mounds of dust billow like cotton across this close-up, lit from above by the nearby star HD 200775, with background and foreground stars dotted throughout. The view shows an area in the northwest of the large Iris Nebula, which seems to be clogged with cosmic dust.

That dust is not like the dust at home. It is made of tiny particles of solid matter, ten to a hundred times smaller than household dust grains. Because the dust scatters the light of the nearby star, the cloud shines by reflected starlight rather than glowing on its own.

Researchers studying the Iris are especially interested in one region, to the left of and slightly above the centre of the image. There, dusty filaments look redder than expected. Such an unexpected colour can hint that the dust grains or the conditions around them are different from what astronomers assume, though the caption does not say what the explanation is.
explore: The image is oriented with north down and east to the right, and the field of view is 3.3 arcminutes. It combines four images taken through blue, green, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha filters.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, combining blue, green, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the faint reflected light from the dust needs long exposures to show up.

alt: Billowing, cotton-like mounds of dust lit from above by a bright star, with stars scattered throughout.

caption: The Tarantula Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Star clusters, glowing gas and thick dark dust crowd this infrared Hubble view of the Tarantula Nebula, sometimes described as a cosmic creepy-crawly because of its spidery look.

The picture comes from the Hubble Tarantula Treasury Project, a programme that is scanning and imaging many of the millions of stars inside the nebula. The goal is to map where the Tarantula's stars are and what they are like. With that census in hand, astronomers can piece together the nebula's skeleton, the starry structure that lies beneath its glowing gas.

Infrared light is the key choice here. It passes through dust more easily than visible light, so stars that would be hidden in an ordinary photograph can be counted and studied. The images were taken with two of Hubble's cameras, Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys, combining near-infrared filters to build up this view. The official caption offers few further details.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: This view uses infrared light, which the eye cannot see, so dust that would block starlight in visible light becomes more see-through.

alt: An infrared view of the Tarantula Nebula with star clusters, glowing gas and thick dark dust.

caption: The Sh2-284 nebula, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: Bright orange and red colours fill this detailed view of the Sh2-284 nebula, captured by the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile.

Sh2-284 is a star formation region. At its centre lies a cluster of young stars nicknamed Dolidze 25, and that cluster is the source of the colours. Its radiation is strong enough to ionise the hydrogen gas in the nebula's cloud, stripping electrons from the atoms. As the atoms recapture electrons, the gas glows, and it is this process that produces the bright orange and red hues seen here.

The picture belongs to a much larger effort, a VST survey that measures hydrogen-alpha light across the southern plane and bulge of our galaxy, headed by Janet Drew of the UK's University of Hertfordshire. Surveys like this one map large stretches of the Milky Way in the light of glowing hydrogen, which makes them good at finding star-forming regions such as Sh2-284. The image also includes ultraviolet and near-infrared filters.

understand.summary: This image comes from OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope, using near-ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The caption says the orange and red come from ionised hydrogen; the full filter-to-colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the data lies outside the range of human vision, and long exposures bring out faint gas that would be invisible by eye.

alt: A nebula glowing bright orange and red around a central cluster of young stars.

caption: The region around DEM L 299 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: A turbulent region surrounds the ring-shaped nebula DEM L 299 in this view. It lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy that orbits our own, not far from the Tarantula Nebula.

The picture was produced by combining three black-and-white images taken in December 2001 with the Wide Field Imager on the ESO/MPG 2.2-metre telescope at the La Silla Observatory. Each image was taken through a different filter, one in ultraviolet light and two tuned to the glow of oxygen and of hydrogen, and they were then combined into colour.

A note for careful viewers: the coloured rings around some of the brighter stars are not real features in space. They are caused by light reflecting inside the telescope's optics. Such artefacts are common in astronomical images and are a reminder that a picture is shaped by the instrument as well as the sky.
explore: The field measures 33.3 by 33.0 arcminutes, with north up and east to the left. Each pixel in the full-resolution version covers 0.238 arcseconds.

understand.summary: This composite from the Wide Field Imager combines an ultraviolet filter with narrow filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet part is invisible to the eye, and the coloured rings around bright stars are reflections in the telescope, not something you would see in the sky.

alt: A turbulent region of glowing gas around a ring-shaped nebula, with coloured rings around some bright stars.

caption: The Orion Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This false-colour picture of the Orion Nebula was built from many individual images taken with the Wide Field Imager on the ESO/MPG 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, on the night of 10 to 11 December 2001.

False colour means each colour stands for a specific filter rather than what an eye would see. Here blue shows a broad blue filter, green shows the glow of oxygen, orange shows hydrogen-alpha light and red shows the glow of sulphur. Because glowing gases give off light at their own characteristic wavelengths, this approach turns the picture into a map of where different elements are shining in the nebula.

The Orion Nebula is a well-known star-forming region, where young stars light up the surrounding gas. The images were first processed by Massimo Robberto of STScI and then combined by Hännes Heyer and Henri Boffin of ESO.
explore: Between 10 and 15 images went into each filter, with total exposures ranging from 21 minutes in blue to 32 minutes each for oxygen and hydrogen and 30 minutes for sulphur. The field covers 34 by 33 arcminutes, with north up and east to the left.

understand.summary: This false-colour composite from the Wide Field Imager assigns B to blue, oxygen [OIII] to green, hydrogen-alpha to orange and sulphur [SII] to red.
understand.eye: An eye would not see these colours; they are assigned to individual elements' glow, and the long exposures reveal much fainter gas than is visible through a telescope.

alt: A false-colour view of the Orion Nebula's glowing gas in blue, green, orange and red.

caption: The Bat Shadow in the Serpens Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: In the upper right of this image, a dark shadow falls across the clouds of the Serpens Nebula, a nursery of young stars roughly 1300 light-years from us. It has been nicknamed the Bat Shadow.

The shadow is cast by the protoplanetary disc around a young star called HBC 672. A protoplanetary disc is a flattened ring of gas and dust around a newborn star, the material from which planets may eventually form. This disc is too small for even Hubble to see directly. But as the star shines, the disc blocks part of its light, projecting a huge shadow onto the cloud in which the star was born, rather like a fly on a lamp casting a giant shadow on a wall.
The shadow is enormous. As seen here, it stretches across approximately 200 times the width of our Solar System. In the upper left, a similar-looking shadow extends from another young star.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using J and H filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the disc itself cannot be seen at all, only its shadow.

alt: Nebula clouds with a large dark shadow in the upper right and a similar shadow in the upper left.

caption: The Lupus 3 region, imaged by ESO's VISTA survey telescope
story: Colourful clouds of gas and dust fill this image of the Lupus 3 region, where new stars are being born.

Star-forming regions like this are usually hidden behind their own dust, which blocks visible light. The picture uses infrared observations instead, and infrared light can pass through the dust far more easily, revealing new details in the star-forming areas that are normally obscured. What looks murky in an ordinary photograph opens up in the infrared.

The data came from the VIRCAM instrument on the VISTA telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile. The observations were made as part of the VISIONS survey, which aims to help astronomers understand how stars form inside these dust-shrouded regions. The image was taken through J, H and Ks filters in the near-infrared. The official caption offers few further details.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image comes from VIRCAM on VISTA, using J, H and Ks filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and in visible light much of this star-forming region would be hidden by dust.

alt: Colourful clouds of gas and dust in the Lupus 3 star-forming region.

caption: The star-forming region N11 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Young stars and clouds of gas spread across this broad vista in our neighbouring galaxy, the Large Magellanic Cloud. The region is catalogued as LHA 120-N 11, or N11 for short, and it counts among the busiest star-forming regions in the nearby Universe.
In regions like N11, clouds of gas collapse into new stars, and the most massive of those stars then light up and reshape the gas around them with their radiation and winds.

The picture was captured with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. It is a mosaic, stitched together from observations at five different positions, and it covers an area about six arcminutes across. Hubble recorded the scene through filters spanning visible light and the near-infrared, including narrow ones tuned to the glow of hydrogen. The official caption offers few further details.

understand.summary: This mosaic comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using visible and near-infrared filters plus narrow filters for hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and long exposures bring out faint gas an eye could not see.

alt: A broad view of young stars and gas clouds in the star-forming region N11.

caption: The stellar nursery Gum 29, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This picture shows the intricate structure of Gum 29, a vast stellar nursery. At its centre lies Westerlund 2, a cluster of young stars.

A stellar nursery is a cloud of gas and dust where new stars are forming. Once young stars like those in Westerlund 2 switch on, their energy lights up the surrounding gas and carves it into complex shapes.

One object deserves a closer look. At the bottom of the cluster sits what appears to be a single star but is actually a system of two stars, and they are among the most massive stars known to astronomers. The picture draws on data from the Wide Field Imager camera on the 2.2-metre Max-Planck/ESO telescope, using blue, visual, red and hydrogen-alpha filters. The official caption gives few further details.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters with a hydrogen-alpha filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so this faint nebula looks much more detailed and colourful here than it would by eye.

alt: A stellar nursery of intricate glowing gas with a cluster of young stars at its centre.

caption: The Lobster Nebula, NGC 6357, imaged by ESO's VISTA survey telescope
story: Huge clouds of glowing gas, laced with threads of dust, surround hot young stars in this infrared landscape from ESO's VISTA telescope. The scene is NGC 6357, a stellar nursery known as the Lobster Nebula, seen here in a new light.

Infrared light changes the view because it passes through dust much more easily than visible light. Stars that are hidden or dimmed in ordinary photographs can shine through, and the structure of the clouds around them looks different. For a stellar nursery, where young stars are often still wrapped in the material that formed them, that is a big advantage.

The image comes from a survey called VVV, short for VISTA Variables in the Vía Láctea. That survey is scanning the Milky Way in an effort to map our galaxy's structure and explain how it formed, so this picture is a by-product of a much larger project. It was recorded through J, H and Ks filters in the near-infrared. The official caption offers few further details about the nebula itself.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from VISTA's VIRCAM camera, taken through J, H and Ks filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and many of the stars seen here would be hidden by dust in visible light.

alt: Glowing clouds of gas and tendrils of dust surrounding hot young stars.

caption: The star formation region NGC 3324, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This view, taken with the Wide Field Imager camera mounted on La Silla's 2.2-metre MPG/ESO telescope, shows NGC 3324, a region where stars are forming.

NGC 3324 is home to several massive, blue-white stars, and their influence is written into the shape of the nebula. Their intense radiation has hollowed out a space in the gas and dust around them, pushing material away and leaving a clearing around them. This is a common pattern in star-forming regions: once big, hot stars are born, they begin to reshape and eventually disperse the cloud that made them.

The same stars are also responsible for the colours. Their ultraviolet radiation makes the gas cloud glow in rich hues, as atoms energised by that light release it again at particular wavelengths. The telescope recorded the scene through broad filters and narrow ones tuned to the glow of oxygen and hydrogen, which help pick out where different gases are shining. The official caption offers few further details.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines V and R filters with narrow filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the glowing gas looks far richer in colour than it would through an eyepiece.

alt: A glowing star-forming region with a cavity carved in its gas and dust by bright blue-white stars.

caption: The Ghost Nebula, IC 63, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows IC 63, nicknamed the Ghost Nebula, about 550 light-years from Earth in the direction of Cassiopeia.

The Ghost is unusual because it belongs to two classes at once. It is a reflection nebula, since its dust reflects the light of a nearby star. It is also an emission nebula, since its gas gives off its own light, specifically hydrogen-alpha radiation, a red glow produced when hydrogen atoms are energised.

Both effects come from the same source: the gigantic star Gamma Cassiopeiae. Its light is scattered by the dust, and its energetic radiation excites the hydrogen gas. But that same radiation is slowly wearing the nebula away, so the Ghost is gradually dissipating. Hubble observed it through a wide range of filters, from ultraviolet through visible to near-infrared light.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from ultraviolet through visible to near-infrared light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Some of the data is ultraviolet or infrared, invisible to the eye, and the nebula is far too faint to see like this by eye.

alt: The Ghost Nebula, a cloud of gas and dust lit by a nearby star.

caption: XZ Tauri, HL Tauri and nearby young stars, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view takes in XZ Tauri, a system of several stars, along with its neighbour HL Tauri and a number of other young stellar objects close by in the constellation Taurus.

XZ Tauri is inflating a hot bubble of gas that spreads into the space around it. That space is filled with bright clumps that are themselves pouring out strong winds and jets. Young stars often do this: as they grow, they fling material outward in narrow jets and broader winds, which crash into the surrounding gas and make it glow.

Together, these objects light up the region and create a dramatic scene. Hubble recorded it through a red filter and a narrow filter tuned to hydrogen-alpha light, the red glow given off by energised hydrogen, which is especially good at picking out jets and shocked gas. The official caption offers few other details, so this image is best read as a snapshot of young stars actively reshaping their surroundings.

understand.summary: This visible-light image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using a red filter and a hydrogen-alpha filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: With only red and hydrogen filters, the colours are a mapping rather than what an eye would see, and the faint jets need long exposures to show.

alt: Young stars with a glowing bubble of gas, bright clumps, winds and jets.

caption: The star formation region Gum 41, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: A red glow fills this view of Gum 41, a cloud of hydrogen and newborn stars. The Wide Field Imager, a camera mounted on La Silla's 2.2-metre MPG/ESO telescope in Chile, took the picture.

The colour has a simple explanation. At the centre of this little-known nebula, brilliant hot young stars pour out energetic radiation. That radiation strips electrons from the surrounding hydrogen atoms, and when the atoms recapture them, they give off light at particular wavelengths, including the characteristic red of hydrogen.

That makes Gum 41 a textbook example of how young stars announce themselves: they light up the gas cloud in which they were born. The telescope recorded the scene through blue, visual and red filters plus one that isolates the glow of hydrogen, which highlights exactly this kind of energised gas. The official caption offers few further details about the region.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters with a hydrogen-alpha filter. The caption says the red hue comes from glowing hydrogen; the full filter-to-colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the red glow is much stronger here than it would appear by eye.

alt: A red-glowing cloud of hydrogen gas with newborn stars at its centre.

caption: The Running Chicken Nebula, IC 2944, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Taken with the Wide Field Imager camera on La Silla's 2.2-metre MPG/ESO telescope, this view features the Running Chicken Nebula, a gas cloud with young stars inside it, lying around 6500 light-years away in the constellation of Centaurus (the Centaur).

Its official names are IC 2944 and the Lambda Centauri Nebula. The odd nickname comes from the shape of its brightest region, which some people see as a bird. The star Lambda Centauri, which gives the nebula one of its names, sits just outside the field of view.

Clouds like this are where stars form. Gas and dust collapse into new stars, and those young stars then light up the surrounding gas with their energetic radiation. The telescope recorded the scene through blue, visual and red filters plus one that isolates the glow of hydrogen, which is especially good at picking out gas energised by young stars. The official caption gives few further details, so the view is best enjoyed as a portrait of a busy stellar nursery with a playful name.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters with a hydrogen-alpha filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the nebula appears much brighter and more colourful here than through an eyepiece.

alt: A cloud of glowing gas and newborn stars, its brightest region shaped somewhat like a bird.

caption: The Rho Ophiuchi star-forming region, imaged by NASA's WISE
story: Here the Rho Ophiuchi star-forming region appears in infrared light, observed by NASA's Wide-field Infrared Explorer, WISE, a space telescope rather than one of ESO's own.

The colours carry a clear meaning. Blue and cyan stand for 3.4- and 4.6-micrometre light, which mostly comes from stars. Green and red show light at 12 and 22 micrometres, which is mostly given off by dust. So the image separates the region into two ingredients: the stars, and the dust clouds among which they are forming.

That split matters because star-forming regions are dusty places. Dust blocks visible light, hiding many young stars, but it also glows in the infrared when warmed. Longer infrared wavelengths therefore trace the dust itself, while shorter ones pick out the stars. A view like this lets astronomers see both the nurseries and their newborns at once. The official caption offers few further details.

understand.summary: This infrared image comes from NASA's WISE. Blue and cyan represent 3.4 and 4.6 micrometres, mostly starlight, while green and red represent 12 and 22 micrometres, mostly glowing dust.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colours are assigned to wavelengths we cannot see.

alt: An infrared view of a star-forming region with stars in blue and cyan and dust in green and red.

caption: The dark cloud Barnard 68, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This colour composite shows the dark cloud Barnard 68, combining images taken in visible and near-infrared light. The observations were made in March 1999 with the 8.2-metre VLT Antu telescope and its FORS1 multimode instrument.
In both visible and near-infrared light, this small cloud lets nothing through. Dust particles inside it block the light of the stars behind, so the cloud itself looks completely dark.

Dark clouds like this are cold, dense concentrations of gas and dust, and they are the kind of places where new stars can eventually form, which is why the release was titled How to become a star. Dust blocks shorter wavelengths of light more strongly than longer ones, so astronomers often study such clouds by comparing how much starlight gets through at different colours. The official caption offers few further details about this particular cloud.

understand.summary: This composite from FORS1 on the Very Large Telescope combines visible and near-infrared images through B, V and I filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye; even so, at these wavelengths the cloud remains completely dark.

alt: The dark cloud Barnard 68, completely opaque in visible and near-infrared light.

caption: The star formation region Messier 17, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This picture shows the rose-coloured star-forming region Messier 17, taken with the Wide Field Imager, a camera on the 2.2-metre MPG/ESO telescope at ESO's La Silla site in Chile.

It counts among the sharpest images of the entire nebula. That combination is harder to achieve than it sounds. A wide view is needed to take in the whole cloud and reveal its full size, but it must also keep fine detail across the landscape of gas clouds, dust and newborn stars, and this image manages both.

Star-forming regions like Messier 17 are clouds of gas and dust in which new stars are taking shape. The young stars light up and sculpt the surrounding gas. The telescope recorded the scene through blue, visual and red filters plus one that isolates the light of hydrogen, the most common element in such clouds. The official caption offers few further details about the region.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters with a hydrogen-alpha filter. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the nebula's rose colour is much more vivid here than it would be by eye.

alt: A rose-coloured nebula of gas clouds, dust and newborn stars.

caption: Part of the supernova remnant SN 1006, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows part of SN 1006, a supernova remnant: the expanding debris left behind when a star exploded.

The picture blends observations from two of Hubble's cameras taken years apart. The Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded the light of hydrogen in February 2006, and the Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 added observations in blue, yellow-green and near-infrared light in April 2008.

The remnant itself shows up only in the hydrogen filter, and in this colour image it was given a red hue. That tells us something about how it glows. As the blast wave from the explosion sweeps through the thin gas between the stars, it energises hydrogen atoms, which then give off light at specific wavelengths. The official caption offers few further details, so this view is best read as a close look at the shock front of an exploded star.

understand.summary: This composite combines hydrogen-light observations from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with blue, yellow-green and near-infrared images from Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. The remnant, visible only in hydrogen light, is shown in red.
understand.eye: The remnant is far too faint to see by eye, and the near-infrared data lie beyond what the eye can detect.

alt: Part of the supernova remnant SN 1006, shown in a red hue.

caption: The stellar nursery Monoceros R2, imaged by ESO's VISTA survey telescope
story: This infrared image shows Monoceros R2, a nearby star formation region roughly 2700 light-years from us in Monoceros (the Unicorn). It was made by the VISTA survey telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory.

The region is a loose grouping of massive, hot young stars. Their light illuminates a collection of reflection nebulae, clouds of dust that shine by scattering the light of nearby stars rather than glowing on their own. All of this is embedded within a large molecular cloud, a cold, dense reservoir of gas and dust of the kind from which stars are born.

Infrared observations suit a region like this. Young stars are often hidden inside the dusty clouds that formed them, and infrared light passes through dust much more easily than visible light, so the view reveals stars and structure that would otherwise stay hidden. The picture was built from exposures in the near-infrared Y, J and Ks bands. The official caption offers few further details about the region's individual features.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from VISTA's VIRCAM camera was built from Y, J and Ks exposures, according to the caption. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each band.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and much of what VISTA sees here would be hidden behind dust in visible light.

alt: An infrared view of a star-forming region with hot young stars lighting reflection nebulae inside a molecular cloud.

caption: The Horsehead Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Like a giant seahorse, the Horsehead Nebula rises from a sea of dust and gas in this close-up, which reveals the intricate structure of the horse's head. At the top left edge sits a bright area: a young star still wrapped in the gas and dust of its birthplace.

Also called Barnard 33, the Horsehead is a cold, dark cloud of dust and gas in Orion. It shows up as a silhouette against the bright nebula IC 434 behind it. Few objects in the sky have been photographed more often.

The scene is slowly changing. Radiation from the young star at top left is eroding the gas and dust in which it was born. In a similar way, a massive star outside Hubble's field of view is shaping the Horsehead's upper edge. The image was released to mark Hubble's eleventh anniversary, and internet voters chose the Horsehead as the object for the telescope to observe.
explore: The picture was produced by the Hubble Heritage Project, and it is a testament to the nebula's popularity that the public picked it for this anniversary view.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, using blue, visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the Horsehead is far too faint to see by eye without a telescope and long exposures.

alt: A dark, horse-head-shaped cloud of dust and gas rising against a brighter nebula, with a bright spot at its top left edge.

caption: The southern part of N44 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
story: This picture shows the southern part of N44, an H II region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy of the Milky Way.

An H II region is a cloud of hydrogen gas that has been ionised by the energetic light of hot, young stars. When the atoms in the gas recapture electrons, they give off light at particular wavelengths, which is why such clouds glow. Regions like this are signposts of recent star formation.

The colours carry a clue. According to the caption, the green areas are particularly hot. The camera, the Wide Field Imager on ESO's 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, recorded the scene through narrow filters that isolate light from oxygen and from hydrogen, so different colours in the image trace different gases and conditions. The field measures 27.5 by 26.5 arcminutes, with north up and east to the left. The official caption offers few further details.

understand.summary: This image from the Wide Field Imager uses narrow filters for two kinds of oxygen light and for hydrogen-alpha. The caption says green marks particularly hot areas; the full filter-to-colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate individual gases rather than showing the colours an eye would see, and long exposures reveal very faint gas.

alt: Glowing gas in the southern part of the N44 region, with green highlighting particularly hot areas.

caption: The supernova remnant SNR 0509-67.5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A delicate shell seems to drift calmly through space in this Hubble image, but the calm is misleading. This bubble, SNR B0509-67.5 or SNR 0509 for short, is what remains visible of a mighty stellar blast in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy roughly 160 000 light-years away.

The gaseous shell formed as the expanding blast wave and debris from the supernova tore through the surrounding interstellar gas. It measures 23 light-years across and is growing at more than 18 million kilometres per hour.

Look closely and you can see ripples in the shell's surface. They may come from small variations in the density of the surrounding gas, or they may be pushed from inside by fragments of the original explosion. The caption leaves both possibilities open, a reminder that even a tidy-looking bubble can hide an unsolved question.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the remnant on 28 October 2006 using a filter that isolates the light of glowing hydrogen in the shell. Those data were combined with visible-light images of the surrounding stars taken by Wide Field Camera 3 on 4 November 2010.

understand.summary: This combines a hydrogen-alpha image of the shell from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with visible and near-infrared images of the star field from Wide Field Camera 3. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The faint glowing shell would be invisible by eye, and part of the star-field data is near-infrared.

alt: A delicate, bubble-shaped shell of gas with rippled edges floating among stars.

caption: The Chameleon I molecular cloud, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A large, dark cloud fills the frame, textured like smoke with wispy gaps in its upper half and fading gently away at the bottom and sides. On the left are several orange stars, three with six large spikes. This is the heart of Chameleon I, a dark molecular cloud 630 light-years away, seen by Webb's NIRCam.

The cold, wispy cloud glows faintly blue in the infrared, lit by the young protostar Ced 110 IRS 4, which appears orange at upper left and is driving an outflow. Many background stars show as orange dots behind the cloud.

Those background stars are the key to the science. As their light passes through the cloud, ices absorb some of it, revealing what the ices are made of. Using this approach, astronomers found a variety of ices in the darkest, coldest parts of any molecular cloud yet measured.
explore: These are the simple icy molecules that could one day be built into future exoplanets. The discovery also opens a new window on how more complex molecules form, the first step toward the building blocks of life.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam shows a 1.5-micron filter in cyan and a 4.1-micron filter in orange.
understand.eye: This light is infrared and invisible to the eye; in visible light, a dark cloud like this simply blocks what lies behind it.

alt: A large, dark, smoke-textured cloud with wispy gaps, several orange stars with six spikes on the left, and many tiny stars on a black background.

caption: The gas clouds NGC 2014 and NGC 2020, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Two glowing clouds of gas sit side by side in this sharp view of a region of star birth in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy orbiting the Milky Way. On the right, NGC 2014 is irregular in shape and red. Its neighbour, NGC 2020, is round and blue.

They look very different, yet both were shaped in the same basic way. Extremely hot newborn stars drive powerful stellar winds that sculpt the surrounding gas. Those same stars also pour radiation into the gas, making it glow brightly.

Why, then, the contrast in shape and colour? The caption does not explain the difference, but the pair shows how the same forces can produce strikingly different results. The Very Large Telescope recorded the scene through broad filters and narrow ones for oxygen and hydrogen.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the FORS2 instrument on the Very Large Telescope, using B, V and R filters plus filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The packet does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures on a large telescope gather much more light than the eye, so these faint clouds look far brighter here than they would by eye.

alt: Two glowing gas clouds side by side: an irregular red cloud on the right and a round blue cloud beside it.

caption: The Vela supernova remnant, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
story: Orange and pink clouds sweep across this view, with bright blue stars scattered in front of them. The clouds are the Vela supernova remnant, the debris left behind after a massive star died in an explosion.

When a massive star explodes, it hurls material outward at great speed. As that debris ploughs into the thin gas between the stars, it compresses and heats it, producing the glowing filaments seen here. The bright blue stars are in the foreground and have nothing to do with the remnant, but they add sparkle to the scene.

The image is huge: 554 million pixels, assembled as a mosaic from observations with the 268-million-pixel OmegaCAM camera on the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory. OmegaCAM can observe through several filters, each passing light of a particular colour. Four were used here, shown as a combination of magenta, blue, green and red, which brings out the fine gaseous filaments in striking detail.

understand.summary: This mosaic comes from OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope. Four filters were used, represented as magenta, blue, green and red, though the packet does not say which filter received which colour.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal filaments far too faint for the eye, and the colours are assigned to filters rather than showing what an eye would see.

alt: Orange and pink filaments of gas sweeping across the frame, with bright blue foreground stars.

caption: The star-forming region Sh 2-106, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Subaru Telescope
story: An hourglass-shaped cloud of gas, full of turbulence, surrounds a dust-shrouded star at the centre of this image. This is Sh 2-106, or S106 for short, a compact star-forming region in the constellation Cygnus (the Swan).

The star at its heart is called S106 IR, and it has only recently formed. Although it is hidden in dust, it shapes the scene around it: it gives the surrounding gas cloud its hourglass-like form and stirs up the turbulence visible within. In this image, light from glowing hydrogen is coloured blue.

The picture is a collaboration between two telescopes. Hubble observations fill the centre, while images from the Subaru Telescope, run by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, extend the field of view around the edges. Combining them gives a wider scene than Hubble's view alone. Much of the data was gathered in near-infrared light, which helps reveal structure that dust would otherwise hide.

understand.summary: This composite combines Hubble Wide Field Camera 3 data in the centre with Subaru Telescope images around the edges, using a hydrogen-alpha filter and several near-infrared filters. The caption says hydrogen light is shown in blue; the rest of the mapping is not published.
understand.eye: An eye would see hydrogen's glow as red, not blue, and most of the data is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see.

alt: An hourglass-shaped cloud of turbulent gas around a dust-shrouded star at the centre, with blue marking glowing hydrogen.
